### Manifesto 2026 commitments (verbatim)

**Digital Technology**: *Technology helping, not harming.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-digital-technology.md))

1. Regulate social media platforms to address harmful content and behaviour by introducing a Digital Duty of Care. This will require algorithmic transparency and accessible and responsive complaints systems, as well as strengthening enforcement with an independent national regulator.
2. Regulate artificial intelligence to ensure its use is safe, transparent and accurate,
3. Crack down on tax avoidance and the offshoring of profits by multinational tech giants such as Meta, Amazon and Microsoft.
4. Adopt and implement the Māori Data Governance Model and Māori AI Governance Framework from Te Kāhui Raraunga across the public sector to protect Māori data sovereignty.
5. Strengthen obligations on data-holders to protect user and biometric data, increase penalties for privacy breaches, and strengthen enforcement powers for the Privacy Commissioner to better protect personal information.
6. Expand media and digital literacy education, and equip New Zealanders to navigate AI-generated media and other emerging digital technologies.
7. Reduce barriers to digital inclusion and ensure all communities have access to the internet, suitable devices and offline alternatives for essential services.

**Small Business**: *Championing small, local enterprise.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-small-business.md))

1. Revitalise ‘Buy Kiwi Made’ and expand country of origin labelling so it’s easier to support local businesses.
2. Commit government departments to buying more goods and services from Aotearoa businesses.
3. Foster sustainable, low-carbon jobs in the information and communication technology sector by expanding access to grants and rebates for smaller sized firms.
4. Continue to invest in community-led regional development with a focus on sustainable building, regenerative agriculture and horticulture, improving low-carbon infrastructure, and iwi- and hapū-led economic activity.
5. Reform competition laws to create a fairer playing field for small businesses and to benefit consumers. Increase the resources and powers of regulatory agencies to investigate anti-competitive practice.

<a id="pol54653"></a>
**Return the tax rate to 33 percent for New Zealand's biggest corporations**  
`POL54653` · topics: incomes-and-employment, economy, tax-and-income-support, business-support

- **Why:** This party says that multi-national businesses send profits offshore and don't pay the same taxes as local businesses. This increases prices and decreases wages. ### Manifesto 2026 commitments (verbatim)

**Income**: *Liveable incomes made possible through a fair tax system.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-income.md))

1. Reform the Social Security Act to uphold the dignity of those who need support and ensure everyone has a secure income and a decent standard of living. Implement a high-trust operating model at Work and Income.
2. Increase benefits to liveable rates, individualise benefit entitlements and abolish benefit sanctions.
3. Extend ACC to cover income support and treatment for injuries, disability and illnesses regardless of origin.
4. Strengthen Working for Families by boosting the rate, reducing abatements and extending tax credits to families who are out of work.
5. Make income tax settings fair and progressive, by introducing a tax-free threshold, reducing tax rates for low- and middle-income earners, and increasing the top rate of income tax.
6. Introduce a super-rich tax of 2.5% on net wealth over $10 million so that multimillionaires pay their fair share.
7. Overhaul recoverable assistance so that grants are available for urgent needs instead of loans. Work towards writing off existing debt to MSD and ban attachment orders against beneficiaries.

**Workforce rights**: *Employment protections and decent pay for all workers.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-workforce-rights.md))

1. Strengthen worker bargaining power by changing employment law to default union membership. This means people automatically join a union when they start a new job, but can opt out later.
2. Expand the right to strike, including for breaches of collective agreements and political and solidarity reasons.
3. Strengthen employment law to protect all workers’ free time with a right to disconnect. Ensure protection from unwanted contact or surveillance out of working hours.
4. Explore legislating to put workers’ representatives on boards of publicly listed companies.
5. Guarantee annual minimum wage increases that at least keep up with inflation. Pay all publicly funded roles a living wage. Work towards matching the minimum wage to the living wage.
6. Increase paid parental leave to 15 months for the primary caregiver, with additional ring-fenced leave for partners, while also increasing payments.
7. Protect platform and gig-economy workers by strengthening the test for whether a worker is a contractor.
8. Close the gender and ethnic pay gaps by undoing the Government’s changes to the pay equity regime and resuming claims, pay transparency measures, and comprehensive pay gap reporting.

### Manifesto 2026 commitments (verbatim)

**Drug Law Reform**: *Putting health first to keep people safe.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-drug-law-reform.md))

1. Repeal and replace the Misuse of Drugs Act with an evidence-based approach that reduces harm, treats drug use as a health issue and provides for regulated access to cannabis for personal use.
2. Ramp up funding of harm reduction and addiction support for people who want to reduce or stop their drug intake, including through kaupapa Māori, rainbow, youth and harm reduction programmes.
3. Work with local government and service providers — focused on safe drug use, addictions and social housing — to support town centres negatively impacted by drug use.
4. Enable a licensing system for psychedelic treatment and recognise taonga status of our native psylocibin (magic mushroom) species.
5. Pass Good Samaritan laws that allow people to call for help without fear of punishment. Legalise and fund other overdose measures including increasing the availability of naloxone and medically supervised consumption spaces to reduce harm and save lives.
6. Fund culturally responsive vaping and smoking cessation services, phase down nicotine availability, and implement stronger regulation and enforcement for nicotine retailers to protect young people and children.
7. Replace the Land Transport (Drug Driving) Amendment Act 2025 with an impairment approach to reduce harm from all causes of driving impairment.
8. Phase out all alcohol advertising and sponsorship, including at sporting and cultural events, and use funding from the alcohol levy to establish a well-resourced national harm-reduction campaign.

**Health**: *Accessible care to support everyone’s good health.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-health.md))

1. Ensure public health care services are accessible for all with a focus on prevention and early screening, diagnosis and treatment for non-communicable diseases, such as kidney disease, cancers, diabetes and cardiovascular and respiratory diseases.
2. Fund mobile health care and mental health care clinics, diagnostics services and dental vans to ensure rural communities are able to access health services regularly, including during and after civil emergencies.
3. Work towards a publicly delivered, fully free provision of dental and primary care services, including by-Māori for-Māori community clinics.
4. Fund one-stop-shops that provides pā harakeke wrap-around services for whānau throughout hapūtanga, after birth, first stages of life, and navigating parenthood.
5. Stop overly prescriptive Hauora service contracts and commit to working with Iwi Māori Partnership Boards and Hauora Māori to simplify and improve funding arrangements for providers of health services for whānau, hapū iwi and hapori.
6. Increase sustained funding for Pharmac so that it can invest in new medicines and health care devices to enhance treatment outcomes and quality of life.
7. Expand the Minor Health Conditions Service to help pharmacies treat common health issues and update the Integrated community pharmacy services agreement to encourage pharmacists to give appropriate medical advice by compensating them fairly.
8. Ensure all health care workers have fair wages, fund pay parity for primary care nurses and hauora providers, and set safe staffing levels to support worker wellbeing and quality of care for patients.
9. Work towards diagnosing and treating endometriosis faster, including by developing formal clinical guidelines for diagnosing and treating endometriosis and other pelvic pain, and by funding specialised clinics across Aotearoa.
10. Increase funding for data and digital infrastructure and capability in the health sector, and regulate and hold private providers of infrastructure to high standards of privacy.

**Mental Health**: *A safe, supportive and accessible care system.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-mental-health.md))

1. Expand free mental health services to all communities so everyone can access support when they need it. This includes expanding youth services like Piki, Mana Ake and Youth One Stop Shops throughout Aotearoa, Asian Family Services and dedicated support for postnatal mental health.
2. Implement the recommendations of the Every Life Matters – He Tapu te Oranga o ia Tangata Suicide Prevention Strategy, together with further actions identified as part of the kaupapa Māori response to suicide prevention with particular focus on people under 24.
3. Implement community care models and ensure mental health facilities are resourced adequately to enable phasing out the use of seclusion (solitary confinement) entirely, and increase the availability of early intervention to reduce the use of compulsory care.
4. Fund kaupapa Māori mental health and addiction programmes and ensure rangatahi Māori voice is represented in policy.
5. Link primary health and secondary mental health services with clear referral pathways in every health region and focus on areas which have disproportionate need.

### Manifesto 2026 commitments (verbatim)

**Education**: *An Aotearoa where everyone can reach their full potential.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-education.md))

**Tertiary Education**: *Opportunities for everyone to learn and grow.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-tertiary-education.md))

1. Support students with a universal student income, including at postgraduate level, and ensure courses that require work placements pay students at least the living wage.
2. Overhaul funding for the tertiary sector to ensure it delivers rigorous research, a wide range of course options, quality teaching, comprehensive student services, decent pay and conditions for staff, and full participation of disabled students.

6. Return to default student union membership and develop a governance model for tertiary organisations in which staff, students, communities and tangata whenua govern together.

<a id="pol54740"></a>
**Phase out synthetic nitrogen fertiliser**  
`POL54740` · topics: environment, economy, health, fresh-water-and-pollution, conservation, agriculture, public-health

- **Why:** This party says that synthetic nitrogen fertiliser is harming our environment by polluting our rivers, lakes and groundwater. Between 1991 and 2019, the use of synthetic nitrogen increased by more than 600%. At the same time, more than a third of monitored groundwater sources saw an increase in nitrate levels. It says that contamination of community water supplies poses a risk to human health.
- **How:** This party would lower the current cap on synthetic nitrogen fertiliser for the dairy industry. This is because the dairy industry uses more than 60% of synthetic nitrogen. It would work with farmers across other sectors to cut fertiliser. There is no timeframe set for the phase-out. It would work alongside the Ministry for Primary Industries to develop a clear implementation plan with milestones and would support regenerative farming initiatives such as the Sustainable Food and Fibre Futures fund.

<a id="pol54744"></a>
**Establish a government backed clean energy loan scheme** ⭐ key policy  
`POL54744` · topics: transport-and-infrastructure, environment, incomes-and-employment, energy, emissions-reduction, prices, key-policies-environment

- **Why:** This party says that this policy would help make household power bills more affordable so people would not have to choose between heating or eating. This party says that since 2021, 100,000 more households cannot afford to heat their home and 76,000 could not pay their bills on time. The easiest way to lower household power is to help people generate and store solar power but most people are barred from this due to the expensive upfront cost of equipment purchase.
- **How:** This party would establish a government-backed loan scheme to enable zero-interest clean energy loans for up to 90% of homeowners. Central government would be a 20 percent shareholder, with participating councils and the Local Government Funding Agency (LGFA) splitting the remaining 80 percent. The Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority (EECA) would implement the scheme.

### Manifesto 2026 commitments (verbatim)

**Climate Action: Emissions Reduction**: *Bold action and solutions that hold polluters to account* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2020-climate-action-emissions-reduction.md))

1. Strengthen the Zero Carbon Act by requiring the government Budget process to be consistent with limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees, gross emissions reduction targets and international commitments.
2. Empower the Climate Change Commission to directly set unit supply in the Emissions Trading Scheme, in line with emissions budgets. Align the government Budget process with the National Adaptation Plan and Emissions Reduction Plans.
3. Introduce a price on agricultural emissions to ensure methane reduction targets are met, with financial and technical support for on-farm emissions reduction.
4. Reform the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) to restore credibility to the market by phasing out the free allocation of units, removing forestry offsetting so the system functions as a genuine ‘cap-and-trade’ system, and redirecting funding from the reformed ETS to an improved Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry Fund.
5. Ensure Aotearoa meets our Paris Agreement commitments through strong domestic action and, if necessary, environmentally and socially responsible initiatives overseas.
6. Improve public transparency on the costs of inaction by including the fiscal impact of the Nationally Determined Contribution obligation in the financial statements.

**Climate Action: Resilience and Adaption**: *Keeping Aotearoa safe and prepared* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-climate-action-resilience-adaptation.md))

1. Ensure climate adaptation planning affirms tino rangatiratanga and upholds the mana motuhake of whānau, hapū and iwi over whenua, wai and taonga by appropriately funding a Māori Climate Resilience Fund.
2. Expand the role of the Natural Hazards Commission to include cover for climate-related weather events and ensure it plays a key role in managing community-led adaptation and retreat.
3. Prioritise long-term, nature-based solutions over short-term engineering solutions, and increase funding for hapū, iwi and community organisations to deliver these.
4. Ensure planning frameworks give effect to the need for climate adaptation in the approach to land and water use, together with supporting ecosystem restoration and conservation.
5. Establish a dedicated fund for central and local government to implement climate adaptation and resilience measures, including funding for partnerships with tangata whenua and community organisations.
6. Scale up support for, and work with, neighbouring countries in the Pacific to adapt to climate change, and advocate for an international agreement on the rights of people displaced by climate change.

**Conservation and Biodiversity**: *Protecting and restoring plants, animals and ecosystems.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-conservation-and-biodiversity.md))

1. Reform conservation and wildlife protection laws to give effect to Te Tiriti, elevate Indigenous-led land stewardship and ensure the conservation management system prioritises halting and reversing nature loss in Aotearoa.
2. Ban new mining on conservation land, including stewardship land.
3. Expand funding for Jobs for Nature – Mahi mō te Taiao to protect our biodiversity and create thousands of regional jobs.
4. Protect all remaining natural wetlands in legislation, including coastal wetlands and estuaries, and implement a plan to restore at least 30% of degraded wetland area, prioritising areas most important for biodiversity recovery and community resilience.
5. Fund Action for Nature, the implementation plan for the biodiversity strategy, and implement national guidance to protect indigenous biodiversity, including the protection of taonga species.
6. Increase overall public conservation funding, including increasing funding and support for the Predator Free 2050 goal.

**Energy**: *Powering Aotearoa with affordable renewable energy.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-energy.md))

1. Put public wellbeing outcomes first in legislation to guarantee the power system works for people, not profits.
2. Establish a renewable energy infrastructure agency to ensure security of supply and lower prices for households, businesses and industry.
3. Increase resilience by enabling greater distributed solar and batteries for households, marae and suitable public buildings, and supporting community-led energy planning.
4. Ban new fossil fuel extraction, end subsidies for fossil fuels and cancel the LNG terminal.
5. Establish a single energy regulator and a Ministry for Energy, focusing on affordable, secure and sustainable energy with equitable access and Te Tiriti-based frameworks that enable Māori and community involvement, ownership and leadership in energy projects.
6. Work with industry to decarbonise and encourage demand response and energy efficiency.

**Environmental Protection**: *Protecting and restoring nature.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-environmental-protection.md))

1. Implement strong evidence-based limits for ecosystem health, secure the role of Te Tiriti and affirm the role of tangata whenua as shared decision-makers and kaitiaki in the new resource management system.
2. Repeal the Fast-track Approvals Act and revoke consents for fast-track approvals for new coal, gold and seabed mining projects.
3. Restore a standalone Ministry for the Environment. Increase resources for the Environmental Protection Authority to identify risks to the environment and human health, and for compliance, monitoring and enforcement to ensure polluters are held accountable.
4. Update air quality standards to bring Aotearoa in line with international standards and to protect human health.
5. Work towards eradication of biosecurity incursions, specifically wilding pines, Caulerpa, and yellow-legged hornets.
6. Re-establish resources for the Community Environment Fund to support grassroots environmental education and action.

**Food Fibre and Forestry**: *A regenerative approach that puts people and nature first.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-food-fibre-and-forestry.md))

1. Increase support for farmers to transition to more sustainable forms of agricultural production through finance mechanisms such as low-interest loans and grants.
2. Back Aotearoa-grown natural fibres, including wool, by using them in the construction and refurbishment of schools and public buildings, and establishing a contestable fund for sustainable fibre manufacturing and innovation.
3. Ban palm kernel expeller and ensure all supplementary feed is sustainably sourced and does not strain the carrying capacity of the local environment.
4. Prevent land from being used beyond its capacities by implementing strong controls on clear-fell of plantation forestry, working to transition extremely erosion-prone land to indigenous forestry and establishing a National Soil Strategy that sets direction on soil use, policies and research.
5. Support the local wood processing sector to manufacture higher-value timber products from plantation forestry, such as cross-laminated timber for construction and turning slash into solid biofuels, retaining regional employment and development.
6. Work with Māori-led forestry organisations to support investment in forestry and restoration of forests on whenua Māori and recognise tangata whenua customary use rights in indigenous forestry according to their tīkanga.
7. Establish a biodiversity credits scheme that supports landowners to undertake restoration and protection of land as a voluntary revenue alternative to the Emissions Trading Scheme. As part of this, prioritise marginal whenua Māori where agreed by landowners.

**Freshwater**: *Healthy water for drinking, swimming and gathering kai.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-freshwater.md))

1. Implement strong, evidence-based national bottom lines for freshwater for both human health and ecosystem health to address pollution including lowering the nitrate limit for drinking water.
2. Reinstate Te Mana o Te Wai to prioritise the health of freshwater in decision-making and regulation and to give effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
3. End all subsidies and public funding for big new irrigation and dam projects and review resource consents where water levels have dropped too far to support a healthy river.
4. Strengthen environmental performance rules for wastewater discharges to ensure lakes, rivers, beaches and coastal areas remain swimmable.
5. Ensure the drinking water regulator is funded and given the mandate for robust and transparent monitoring, reporting and enforcement in the protection of drinking water sources.
6. Support greater resilience from floods by increasing funding for adaptation and allowing for a ‘room for rivers’ approach and using natural systems like wetlands to protect communities.
7. Phase out synthetic nitrogen fertiliser and take action to reduce stocking rates on a catchment basis to improve the health of rivers and drinking water and reduce climate pollution.

**Oceans and Fisheries**: *Abundant oceans teeming with kaimoana.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-oceans-and-fisheries.md))

1. Protect at least 30% of New Zealand’s ocean territory by 2030 through reforming marine protected areas legislation to ensure it is fit for purpose and enables both tikanga-led tools consistent with Te Tiriti, and approaches to improve ocean health outcomes.
2. Phase out damaging fishing methods, starting by banning bottom trawling on seamounts, and banning set netting and dredging.
3. Ban seabed mining in the coastal marine area and the exclusive economic zone and maintain pressure for a moratorium on seabed mining in international waters.
4. Embed kaitiakitanga Māori in marine policy and operational management. Resource iwi and hapū to lead oceans protection and implement mātauranga- and tikanga-based projects for ocean conservation.
5. Reduce fisheries bycatch of protected species by ensuring cameras are rolled out on the entire fishing fleet and by setting fisheries-related mortality limits.
6. Ratify the Agreement on Marine Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction and support marine protection proposals in the high seas, Southern Ocean and throughout the Pacific.
7. Review the Quota Management System and move towards an ecosystem-based fisheries management model, in line with the Māori fisheries settlements.

**Welfare of Animals**: *Caring for all animals that call Aotearoa home.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-welfare-of-animals.md))

1. Create a new Commissioner for Animals to independently monitor and advocate for the rights of animals, and an independent ministry.
2. Resource the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee to ensure all animal welfare codes genuinely comply with the Animal Welfare Act, and introduce stronger codes for farmed animals.
3. Phase out harmful activities including debeaking of hens, intensive winter grazing, factory farming, octopus farming, farrowing crates and rodeo.
4. Require that imported products meet the animal welfare standards of Aotearoa, including for cosmetics.
5. Introduce consistent, clear and enforceable standards for manufacturing claims about animal welfare and ingredients (such as ‘free range’, ‘cruelty free’ and ‘vegan’).
6. Retain the ban on live exports of farmed animals by sea and extend the ban to include live exports of farmed animals by air and wild-caught animals such as endangered tuna longfin eels.

**Zero Waste**: *Building a sustainable circular economy.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-zero-waste.md))

1. Establish strong product policy measures, including mandatory product stewardship, a beverage container return scheme, phase-outs of problematic products and comprehensive right-to-repair.
2. Direct revenue from the waste disposal levy into waste minimisation initiatives and stop diverting the local government portion to other purposes. Increase the levy to match international best practice and apply a consistent rate across all landfill classes.
3. Introduce a moratorium on waste-to-energy plants and explore energy generation from biogas associated with animal and plant wastes.
4. Build on proposed reforms of the Waste Minimisation Act to implement timely, binding, measurable and ambitious waste reduction targets. Ensure legislation gives effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Introduce comprehensive duty-of-care systems for the waste and resource recovery sector covering all waste streams, including hazardous waste.
5. Make greater use of discarded soil. Divert soil from landfills, where safe and appropriate to do so.
6. Prioritise local, mana whenua and community-driven solutions to resource recovery, implementation of national zero-waste strategies, and organic waste reduction, diversion and processing.

### Manifesto 2026 commitments (verbatim)

**Transport**: *Easy, sustainable ways to get around.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-transport.md))

1. Transform public transport networks, including building mass rapid transit in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, and providing comprehensive bus lanes in all cities.
2. Invest in nationwide rapid rail for passengers and freight to connect regions and major cities and contribute to economic development and decarbonisation.
3. Introduce targeted subsidies for e-cargo bikes. Introduce e-bike sharing schemes in community hubs, to allow more families to save on transport costs.
4. Fund affordable, reliable, interregional rural bus services, and on-demand public transport, including by-Māori for-Māori public transport to serve kōhanga reo and rural schools.
5. Extend Community Connect to provide free fares for students and apprentices, community service card holders, everyone under 18, and all Total Mobility card holders.
6. Enable the provision of transport services publicly instead of for profit by replacing the Public Transport Operating Model.
7. Create safe walking and biking routes to all community hubs including schools through building more bike lanes and safe crossings, and lowering speed limits near schools.
8. Implement a phase-out date for the import of fossil-fuel powered vehicles, build more EV (electric vehicle) charging stations, remove regulatory barriers to EV car-sharing and re-introduce incentives for EV uptake.

### Manifesto 2026 commitments (verbatim)

**Māori Centred**: *By Māori, for Māori.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-maori-centred.md))

1. Devolve power and redistribute resources back to tangata whenua in recognition that Māori are the decision-makers and facilitators of the destiny of their own whānau, hapū and iwi.
2. Invest in outcomes that minimise the disparities and inequities tangata whenua face across the majority of social and economic outcomes.
3. Resource marae through a Marae Resilience Fund for Māori to lead initiatives for their people, wāhi tapu (sacred sites) and whenua in accordance with their own tikanga. Create ongoing funding for provisions for civil emergencies in recognition of being consistent community lifelines.
4. End perpetual leases on whenua Māori and amend the Public Works Act to prevent the acquisition of Māori freehold land, Māori customary land and lands within a reasonable proximity to marae, urupā and wāhi tapu.
5. Expand the learning, speaking and promotion of te reo Māori in both formal and informal settings to encourage the widespread use of the language across the nation.

**Te Tiriti o Waitangi**: *Advancing an Aotearoa that embraces Te Tiriti.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-te-tiriti-o-waitangi.md))

1. Amend the Treaty of Waitangi Act to recognise that Te Tiriti is the authoritative text and that Te Tiriti works in conjunction with He Whakaputanga o te Rangatiratanga o Nu Tireni.
2. Implement genuine Te Tiriti-based decision-making models across government and resource iwi and hapū to participate as partners rather than as advisors.
3. Reform the Treaty Settlements process by amending the settlement policy guide for negotiators to enable fair negotiations and just reparations without ceding sovereignty, removing any clauses that refer to ‘Full and Final settlement’, ending the ‘large natural grouping’ approach to Treaty settlements, and validating hapū rangatiratanga.
4. Increase resourcing for the Waitangi Tribunal, providing them with the power to make binding recommendations for the return of Crown and Private land to iwi, whānau and hapū.
5. Facilitate the return of whenua outside of Treaty Settlements that was wrongfully alienated from tangata whenua, including through exploring a right-of-first-refusal process that enables the return of private land to iwi, hapū and whānau at point of sale.

### Manifesto 2026 commitments (verbatim)

**Children**: *Thriving tamariki and rangatahi.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-childen.md))

1. Legislate so that the child’s voice is central in all decisions that matter to them by using the Child Impact Assessment Tool consistently and fully incorporating the Rights of the Child into legislation.
2. Increase the Best Start payment and extend it to every child under three as a universal child benefit for the early years.
3. Elevate workforce safety by funding training and a workforce development strategy prioritising Māori, Pacific, rainbow, disabled and community provider pathways.
4. Improve access to both diagnosis and support services for children with disabilities or learning support needs.
5. Amend the Oranga Tamariki Act so that it protects tamariki Māori and explicitly embeds whānau participation in decision-making to exercise iwi or hapū authority.

**Disability**: *An accessible Aotearoa for all.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-disability.md))

1. Introduce a disability rights law based on Te Tiriti with enforceable accessibility standards.
2. Provide easily accessible and timely income support to meet all disability-related living and medical costs, regardless of relationship status and cause of disability.
3. Address homelessness and work towards all disabled people being able to live in safe, accessible, affordable housing in the community of their choice, including by setting robust universal design standards for public and private housing.
4. Make getting around accessible, including by continuing to fund the 75% subsidy for the Total Mobility taxi scheme, making it easier to use and increasing the number of mobility vehicles to meet demand.
5. Draw on the Enabling Good Lives approach to guide how government agencies work with disabled people. Remove barriers to accessing the essentials like health care, transport, inclusive education and disability support for all who need it.
6. Ensure national and local emergency response plans address the needs of disabled people.
7. Uphold legal capacity for everyone, moving from legal capacity assessments to rights-based systems of supported decision-making.

**Gender Equity**: *For a more equal Aotearoa.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-gender-equity.md))

1. Close the gender and ethnic pay gaps by undoing the Government’s changes to the pay equity regime and resuming claims, pay transparency measures, and comprehensive pay gap reporting.
2. Increase the Best Start payment and extend it to every child under three as a universal child benefit for the early years.
3. Fund one-stop-shops that provides pā harakeke wrap-around services for whānau throughout hapūtanga, after birth, first stages of life, and navigating parenthood.
4. Work towards diagnosing and treating endometriosis faster, including by developing formal clinical guidelines for diagnosing and treating endometriosis and other pelvic pain, and by funding specialised clinics across Aotearoa.
5. Resource kaupapa Māori solutions and community-led solutions to family and sexual violence, that have have been developed by disproportionately impacted groups, including women, Pasifika, rainbow, and disabled communities.
6. Amend the Crimes Act to criminalise coercive control, amend the definition of consent, and preclude a defence of reluctant consent to affirm that consent must be free and voluntary, and can be withdrawn at any time while ensuring these changes cause no further harm.
7. Increase paid parental leave to 15 months for the primary caregiver, with additional ring-fenced leave for partners, while also increasing payments.

**Pacific Peoples**: *Deepening connections and uplifting communities.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-pacific-peoples.md))

1. Extend visa-free travel to Aotearoa for visitors from the Pacific Islands.
2. Restore and increase the international climate aid funding Aotearoa contributes. Affirm and support calls by Pacific Island nations for stronger climate action in international negotiations.
3. Resource tangata moana leadership on climate action within Aotearoa.
4. Replace the Recognised Seasonal Employer Scheme with an alternative that gives Pacific workers access to fair wages, housing and essential services, and provides for open work rights and residency pathways rather than being tied to a single employer.
5. Support the independence of West Papua and French-occupied Polynesia. Call for an Indigenous-led human rights investigation and a visit from the Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.
6. Support Pacific Island states with their marine protection initiatives, including by increasing funding support for the South Pacific Regional Environment Programme and supporting marine protected areas in the Pacific Ocean under the High Seas Treaty.

**Rainbow Communities**: *Rainbow communities thriving with freedom, equality and respect.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-rainbow-communities.md))

1. Work with the different rainbow communities to develop appropriate health care services and strategies built cultural values and holistic models of care and wellbeing.
2. Increase resourcing for rainbow organisations, including dedicated support for Māori and Pasifika-led organisations, to support the development and delivery of services that reflect the diverse needs, values, and strengths of rainbow communities.
3. Resource clear pathways for timely, free, non-discriminatory access to all forms of gender-affirming health care based on informed consent and self-determination, including reversal of the ban on puberty blockers.
4. Promote the human rights of takatāpui, intersex and rainbow people, amending the Human Rights Act to clarify that all forms of sexual orientation, gender identity and variations in sex characteristics, are prohibited grounds of discrimination, and implement the Law Commission’s Ia Tangata report recommendations.
5. Prohibit all non-consensual and medically unnecessary surgeries or medical interventions on intersex people.
6. Reform laws and policies so rainbow asylum seekers, refugees and migrants can access legal gender recognition, partnership recognition, family reunification, and resettlement support.

**Seniors**: *Happy, healthy and supported.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-seniors.md))

1. Launch a dedicated long-term strategy for the needs of an ageing population which encompasses the holistic wellbeing of kaumātua, elder abuse prevention, ensuring income is equitably accessed and sufficient to live comfortably, and the establishment of a state-owned, not-for-profit retirement village scheme.
2. Increase funding for community spaces and the establishment of facilities, programmes, education and volunteering opportunities that are accessible to seniors.
3. Expanding housing options by building more papakāinga, prioritising kaumātua on social housing waitlists, and ensuring housing designs are suitable for their needs — single-level and warm, with mobility features and room for intergenerational living.
4. Ensure support services are grounded in cultural values, and that home and community care workers are well trained, supported and paid equitably and fairly by including travel time.
5. Resource Māori, Pacific and migrant organisations to provide kaumātua care that is aligned with their values, cultural practices and tikanga.

**Democracy**: *Politics for people, not big money.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-democracy.md))

1. Resource a national conversation for constitutional transformation that upholds He Whakaputanga and Te Tiriti o Waitangi as our founding constitutional documents, utilising Matike Mai Aotearoa to facilitate community discussions.

4. Reform electoral funding by limiting donations to registered voters, increasing public financing of campaigns and capping a donor’s donations at a level that does not risk donor influence over policy.
5. Strengthen the rules and transparency over political lobbying, including through a lobbyist register and a code of conduct.

**Justice and Community Safety**: *Keeping communities safe through prevention and rehabilitation.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-justice-and-community-safety.md))

1. Resource evidence-based rehabilitation for anyone convicted of an offence, and ensure tikanga-based and restorative justice solutions (such as Te Pae Oranga) are available to anyone who wishes to access these.
2. Expand Te Ao Mārama to all courts in Aotearoa, and ensure specialist youth courts including the Rangatahi and Pasifika Courts, Alcohol and Other Drug Treatment Court, and New Beginnings Court are available to all who wish to access them.
3. End military-style academies, raise the age of criminal responsibility and ban the detention of young people in the company of adults in all circumstances.
4. Require body cameras for frontline police, strengthen powers for the Independent Police Conduct Authority, deliver de-escalation and trauma training for police, and increase resourcing for Māori Wardens and Pacific Wardens.
5. Improve community reintegration support for people leaving the criminal justice system, including housing, and increase the Steps to Freedom Grant to cover at least 30 years of inflation.
6. Extend legal aid and duty lawyers, better resource community law centres and make applications for protection and parenting orders free.
7. Enable judicial discretion in sentencing, including by abolishing mandatory minimum sentences, life sentences, preventive detention, limits on sentence discounts, three strikes and limits on when home detention can be imposed instead of imprisonment.
8. Implement the recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the Terrorist Attack on Christchurch Mosques on 15 March 2019. Extend hate speech laws to cover religion, gender, disability and rainbow communities. Continue to oppose possession of military-style semi-automatic firearms.
9. Implement all recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care, in consultation with people with lived experience.

**Local Government**: *Empowering local democracy.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-local-government.md))

1. Strengthen local electoral democracy by transferring administration of local government elections to the Electoral Commission, enabling 16-year-olds to vote and requiring the use of a single transferable voting system.
2. Reinforce councils’ responsibility to give effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi by making the role of local government as a Te Tiriti partner explicit, and reinstate their ability to keep Māori wards for their districts.
3. Reject the proposed rates cap and enable a range of new funding and financing tools, such as a bed levy, congestion charging and GST from rates and growth.
4. Ensure that the ‘four wellbeings’ (social, economic, environmental and cultural) are core to the purpose of local government and empower councils by devolving further responsibilities from central government, with appropriate resourcing.
5. Enable greater use of community-based decision-making processes — such as citizens’ assemblies — including greater community input in the process for local government reorganisation.

**Public Services**: *Strong essential services accessible to everyone.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-public-services.md))

1. Uphold Te Tiriti throughout the work of the public service, and fund Māori organisations, iwi, hapū and marae to run community and environmental initiatives that meet the needs and aspirations unique to their rohe (region).
2. Fund public services adequately to ensure that they are able to work in service of the public good, and that public services (and state-owned enterprises) remain in public hands.
3. Reform the public finance system to ensure that the fiscal management approach supports New Zealand’s long-term resilience, the productive capacity of our economy, and an ensures the health and well-being of everyone.
4. Affirm the importance of advocacy and monitoring done by independent commissions with expertise in an area, starting with restoring the monitoring role of the Children’s Commissioner alongside its advocacy function.
5. Introduce standardised career progression, pay, community secondment opportunities and training across the public sector to improve staff retention and skills development, and ensure equal pay for equivalent roles.
6. Provide secure, flexible and full funding arrangements for the community sector, recognising the value of the work, and ensuring independence within a supportive legislative framework.
7. Improve training in Te Tiriti and te reo Māori for all public servants, resulting in consistency across all agencies.
8. Ensure that the public service is a leader in disability-responsive employment, including by providing resources and training to meet access needs and counter ableism.

**Violence Prevention**: *Keeping whānau and communities safe.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-violence-prevention.md))

1. Fund the implementation of the action plan for Te Aorerekura: National Strategy to Eliminate Family Violence and Sexual Violence, centred on Te Tiriti.
2. Resource kaupapa Māori solutions and community-led solutions to family and sexual violence, that have have been developed by disproportionately impacted groups, including women, Pasifika, rainbow, and disabled communities.
3. Prioritise violence responses and prevention by improving workforce and broader public understanding of the drivers and signs of violence, and how to respond in ways that enhance safety and healing.
4. Amend the Crimes Act to criminalise coercive control, amend the definition of consent, and preclude a defence of reluctant consent to affirm that consent must be free and voluntary, and can be withdrawn at any time while ensuring these changes cause no further harm.
5. Restore relationship and sexuality teaching guidelines — including education on healthy relationships, diverse identities and sexualities, and affirmative consent — in all schools.
6. Increase funding for counselling and mental health support for victims, whānau, witnesses, defendants and legal professionals engaging in the justice system.

### Manifesto 2026 commitments (verbatim)

**Immigration and Community Safety**: *Welcoming, safe and fair pathways to make Aotearoa home.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-immigration-and-refugees.md))

1. Create residence pathways for migrants who have settled long-term, including for people living in Aotearoa whose visas have expired.

**Overseas New Zealanders**: *Cultivating Kiwi connections around the world.* ([full chapter](documents/web-manifesto-2026-overseas-new-zealanders.md))

1. Enable a tikanga-based pathway for people who whakapapa Māori to establish Aotearoa citizenship, regardless of country of residence or birth.
2. Reduce and re-balance student loan repayments and interest rates for overseas student loan borrowers, extend the repayment holiday for overseas borrowers, and abolish border arrests for student loan repayment violations.
3. Extend the time that overseas New Zealanders can spend outside Aotearoa without losing voting eligibility.
4. Restore the 10-year period for time spent in Aotearoa New Zealand to be eligible for superannuation.
5. Pursue reciprocal health care, welfare support and visa waiver arrangements with other countries, and widen existing agreements to include temporary visitors.

# Labour Party: 2026 election policies

Every 2026 election policy of the New Zealand Labour Party that this archive could find, with summaries and links to the **full verbatim text** of every source page.

- **126 policies** in total: **76** listed by [policy.nz](https://policy.nz) (summaries by policy.nz, marked *policy.nz*) and **50** more found on labour.org.nz that policy.nz does not list separately (summaries written for this archive, marked *archive*).
- **138 full-text source documents** in [`documents/`](documents/): Labour's policy pages, PDFs, press releases and speeches on labour.org.nz, plus Scoop, RNZ and TVNZ pages that policy.nz cited. All were fetched from the original URLs (web.archive.org links in policy.nz were mapped back to the original pages) on **23 October 2026**. Text is verbatim; only the markup was turned into Markdown. Six policy PDFs (factsheets and policy documents linked from Labour pages) are also included as extracted text, and the PDFs themselves are kept in `raw/party-docs/labour/pdf/`.
- Structured data: [`policies.json`](policies.json). Scripts: `tools/policies_labour_fetch.py`, `tools/policies_labour_extract.py`, `tools/policies_labour_build.py`.
- How completeness was checked: every policy card on Labour's policy hub ([labour.org.nz/policy](https://www.labour.org.nz/policy)) and every page linked from it was captured. labour.org.nz has no sitemap.xml (it returns 404), so the list of all ~820 news items in the site's news menu was used instead: the ~300 most recent titles (roughly August 2025 to 22 October 2026) were read one by one and older ones were searched by keyword, and every release that announced a commitment was captured. Releases that only attack other parties, or report member's bills that have already passed, are not counted as policies.
- Each *archive* summary is a neutral restatement of what the linked Labour text says. Costings are Labour's own figures; none are independent estimates. Where sources disagree, this is noted.

## Headline commitments

These are the policy cards on Labour's [policy hub](https://www.labour.org.nz/policy), in Labour's order. Each description is Labour's own text (full page: [documents/policy.md](documents/policy.md)).

- **$20 Fare Cap**: $20 a week is the most you'll pay to get around by bus or train under Labour. In place by 1 July 2027.
- **Free Doctor's Visits**: Three free doctor's visits a year for everyone. Delivered with Labour's new Medicard.
- **Free Prescriptions**: Labour will remove the $5 fee on prescriptions to make them free for everyone. From 1 July 2027.
- **Free Maternity Scans**: Labour will make maternity scans free, everywhere in New Zealand with the Medicard. From July 2028.
- **Free Cervical Screening**: With Labour's Medicard, cervical screening will be free for ages 25-69. From 1 October 2027.
- **ED Recovery Plan**: Free GP visits, free prescriptions, more nurses and faster emergency care to ease pressure on emergency departments.
- **Family Doctor Loan Scheme**: Labour's Family Doctor Loan Scheme supports local GPs to buy into practices and stay in their communities. From 1 July 2027.
- **New Zealand Future Fund**: Backing New Zealand's potential and investing in a future made in New Zealand.
- **Capital Gains Tax**: A simple, targeted 28% tax on profit from selling investment property after 1 July 2027. Nine in 10 New Zealanders won't pay it.
- **Apprenticeship Boost**: Labour will support more tradies with extended employer payments, a $1,000 toolbox grant, and five new trades covered. From 1 July 2027.
- **SolarSaver**: Labour's SolarSaver is a fully-funded programme to help homeowners, renters and communities get solar without the upfront cost.
- **Small Business Action Plan**: Getting small business owners paid sooner, easier ways to invest, and less paperwork.
- **Small Business First**: A fair shot at work and less time dealing with the government.
- **Fiscal Plan**: Balance the books, return to surplus by 2028/29, reduce net debt towards 20% of GDP, and keep government spending and revenue sustainable.
- **AI in New Zealand's Interests**: Protect what matters, unlock our potential, and lead on our own terms with a new Office of AI and a framework to recognise and pay creators when AI uses their work.
- **Backing Māori into Skilled Work**: Māori-led training that helps more whānau Māori gain skills and move into good, well-paid work.
- **Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee**: Every eligible New Zealand-trained graduate nurse will be offered a job in our health system, from 2027.
- **Strengthening KiwiSaver**: Compulsory employer contributions rising to 6% by 2032, plus support during parental leave and over-65s.
- **Banning Price Gouging**: Making it illegal for big companies to overcharge for essentials.
- **Fairer Grocery Prices**: More competition, more choice, fairer prices by breaking open the supermarket duopoly's grip on wholesale supply.
- **Start Work Now**: Building homes, fixing schools and repairing hospitals - getting Kiwis back on the tools and nearly 30,000 apprentices into work.
- **Cutting Student Debt**: A 10% cut to eligible student loan balances, with small balances under $2,000 written off completely.
- **A Fair Go For Families**: No hidden fees. No traps. No rip-offs. Banning junk insurance and making cancelling as easy as signing up.
- **Pay Equity**: Restoring pay equity legislation and giving an immediate pay rise to care and support workers.
- **A Fair Go For Drivers**: Fairer fuel pricing, a right to repair law for cars, and a fairer deal at the car yard.
- **Fuel Tax Freeze**: Labour will freeze fuel excise tax for three years, saving an average family $520 a year by 2030.
- **Banking for Everyone**: Opening up banking competition, backing Kiwi fintech with a new digital banking licence, and keeping Kiwibank 100% New Zealand-owned.
- **A Better Deal When You Fly**: Real prices upfront, automatic refunds when things go wrong, and more airlines competing for your business.
- **Cutting Back-to-School Costs**: Cheaper uniforms, healthy school lunches back from Term 1 2028, rural school buses restored, and lower transport costs.
- **Keeping Kids off Screens**: Kids being kids for longer: sport grants, after-school activities, clearer screen rules in schools and support for parents.
- **Safer Online**: Basic rules for big tech: no social media for under-16s, more control over your feed, and a Digital Duty of Care.

## Fiscal plan and costings

Labour published its Fiscal Plan on 4 October 2026 ([labour.org.nz/fiscal-plan](https://www.labour.org.nz/fiscal-plan), full text: [documents/fiscal-plan.md](documents/fiscal-plan.md)). Its earlier fiscal strategy page is at [documents/fiscal-strategy.md](documents/fiscal-strategy.md). The key facts as Labour states them:

- Every election commitment is fully costed and fully funded, independently reviewed by Hall Chadwick
- Books return to an OBEGAL surplus in 2028/29
- Net debt down towards 20% of GDP over time
- Operating allowance held at $2.4 billion per Budget, as set at Budget 2026
- $12 billion in future capital allowances; Labour's commitments use $4.1 billion, leaving almost $8 billion unallocated
- $15.5 billion of additional health funding over the forecast period

Capital commitments (from the Fiscal Plan page):

Labour's announced capital commitments fit comfortably within the $12 billion of future capital allowances, leaving almost $8 billion unallocated.

| Commitment | Capital funding |
| --- | --- |
| New Zealand Future Fund | $200 million |
| Student loan write-off | $420 million |
| Hospitals | $200 million |
| Schools | $400 million |
| Kainga Ora housing (over four years) | $2.9 billion |
| Ratepayer Assistance Scheme solar expenditure | $7 million |

Costings listed on Labour's policy hub FAQ ("How are Labour's policies being funded?"), verbatim:

- free prescriptions: $74.5 million a year
- free maternity scans: $28.6 million a year
- free cervical screening: $21.6 million a year
- Apprenticeship Boost: an average of $56.5 million a year over four years
- SolarSaver: $160 million over four years
- Backing Māori into Skilled Work: $21 million a year
- the Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee: $525 million
- the Small Business Action Plan: $1.56 billion over four years, funded by refocusing Investment Boost
- Start Work Now: around $450 million for schools, $200 million for hospitals and $2.9 billion in capital for housing
- Pay equity is funded within Labour's Fiscal Plan, with future settlements funded through future Budgets as agreements are reached.
- The $950 million Crown guarantee for the Community Housing Funding Agency would only be called on in the unlikely event of a default.

> Note on timing: policy.nz (citing Labour's August fiscal strategy page) gives the OBEGAL surplus year as 2029/30. Labour's Fiscal Plan of 4 October 2026 says 2028/29.

## Health

### Remove $5 charge for prescriptions

`POL54665` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Incomes & employment

**Why:** This party says that that last year, 155,000 New Zealanders didn't collect medicine they had been prescribed because they couldn't afford it. Not receiving treatments mean that health problems are exacerbated, and research shows that people who skip medication are more likely to end up in hospital. Making prescriptions free is an upfront cost for the government which removes pressure on the health system.

**How:** This party would remove the $5 fee for prescriptions of funded medication. This would apply to anyone who is entitled to free healthcare in New Zealand, instead of just people under age 14 and over age 65 and those with Community Services Cards. This would cost $74.5m a year, funded by a capital gains tax. This party estimates that this policy would cost $74.5 m a year.

**Costing (as stated):** This would cost $74.5m a year, funded by a capital gains tax. This party estimates that this policy would cost $74.5 m a year.

**Full text:** ['Free Prescriptions Under Labour', undated (accessed 11 August 2026)](documents/prescriptions.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/prescriptions)); [Affordable Healthcare - NZ Labour's Medicard Plan](documents/affordable-healthcare.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/affordable-healthcare))

### Make up to three GP visits a year free

`POL54669` · summary: *policy.nz*

**Why:** This party says that many New Zealanders have to choose between medical care and other essentials like food. Some general practices charge nearly $100 per visit. Under the "Medicard" policy programme, anyone eligible for funded healthcare could go to the GP for free at least three times a year. This would be paid for by a capital gains tax.

**How:** This party would cover three visits a year to a doctor or nurse at the GP clinic where people are enrolled. Already free services like immunisations would not count towards the three-visit total. The "Medicard" card and app would link visits to people's National Health Index number. The three free visits are for each year and do not accumulate and roll over into the next year. This party estimates that this policy would cost $393.3 million in 2027/28, rising to around $553 million a year once fully in place.

**Costing (as stated):** This party estimates that this policy would cost $393.3 million in 2027/28, rising to around $553 million a year once fully in place.

**Full text:** ['Free Doctor's Visits with the Medicard', undated (accessed 11 August 2026)](documents/medicard.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/medicard)); [Affordable Healthcare - NZ Labour's Medicard Plan](documents/affordable-healthcare.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/affordable-healthcare)); [Labour's ED Recovery Plan](documents/ed-recovery-plan.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/ed-recovery-plan)); [Labour: Free doctor's visits (Medicard) - PDF](documents/pdf-labour-free-doctors-visits.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/media/vtbneplb/labour-free-doctors-visits.pdf))

### Ensure all referred maternity scans are free

`POL54686` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Community & inclusion

**Why:** This party says that that pregnant people should not have to worry about money to know their baby is healthy, with each scan currently costing an average $90. No mum would have to skip a scan because they can't afford it.

**How:** This party would make every referred maternity scan by a doctor, midwife or specialist free in NZ. All a pregnant person would need is a Medicard. To grow the relevant workforce and ease the pressure on hospitals, 24 paid trainee sonographer positions would also be funded, costing less than $3 million a year. This policy would be funded by the party's targeted capital gains tax. This party estimates that this policy would cost $28.6 million a year.

**Costing (as stated):** To grow the relevant workforce and ease the pressure on hospitals, 24 paid trainee sonographer positions would also be funded, costing less than $3 million a year. This party estimates that this policy would cost $28.6 million a year.

**Full text:** ['Free Maternity Scans with Medicard', undated (accessed 11 August 2026)](documents/maternityscans.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/maternityscans)); [Release: Labour to make maternity scans free](documents/release-labour-to-make-maternity-scans-free.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/news/release-labour-to-make-maternity-scans-free/))

### Implement free cervical screening for everyone aged 25-69

`POL54689` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Community & inclusion

**Why:** This party says that that cervical cancer is one of the most preventable cancers but 85 percent of those diagnosed have never been screened or have missed screenings. Free cervical screening means earlier diagnosis, less pressure on hospitals and more lives saved.

**How:** This party would implement free cervical screening for everyone aged 25-69 from 1 October 2027. People's eligibility would be automatically loaded onto the Medicard, with screening available at their local doctor or community screening event. This would be funded from existing health budgets and would be in addition to the three free doctor's visits a year. This party estimates that this policy would cost $21.6 million for the first full year.

**Costing (as stated):** This party estimates that this policy would cost $21.6 million for the first full year.

**Full text:** ['Free Cervical Screening', undated (accessed 13 August 2026)](documents/cervicalscreening.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/cervicalscreening)); [Release: Labour will make cervical screening free](documents/release-labour-will-make-cervical-screening-free.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/news/release-labour-will-make-cervical-screening-free/)); [Labour: Free cervical screening factsheet - PDF](documents/pdf-cervical-screening-factsheet.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/media/prhel1zq/cervical-screening-factsheet.pdf))

### Provide loans to support local GPs to buy into practices

`POL54692` · summary: *policy.nz*

**Why:** This party says that doctors cannot always afford to buy their own practice. Yet private family doctors form the bulk of general practitioners in the health system. If more GPs can afford to open a practice in their local community, it will lower waiting times to see doctors and ease the pressure on busy hospitals.

**How:** This party would introduce a Family Doctor Loan Scheme providing up to 90% of the cost of buying into a practice. This would cap at $500,000 and would be interest-free for the first two years. A 3 percent annual interest rate would apply after that, with 10 years allowed to repay. Up to 50 loans would be available per year for owner-operated general practices. Funding would be supplied through the existing Small Business Cashflow Loan Scheme. This party estimates that this policy would cost $25 million a year if fully subscribed.

**Costing (as stated):** This party estimates that this policy would cost $25 million a year if fully subscribed.

**Full text:** ['Backing Your Family Doctor', undated (accessed 13 August 2026)](documents/familydoctorloanscheme.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/familydoctorloanscheme)); [Release: Labour backs family doctors](documents/release-labour-backs-family-doctors.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/news/release-labour-backs-family-doctors/)); [Labour: Backing local doctors (Family Doctor Loan Scheme) - PDF](documents/pdf-backinglocaldoctors.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/media/dbskvb1y/backinglocaldoctors.pdf))

### Guarantee jobs for NZ-trained graduate nurses

`POL54820` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Incomes & employment

**Why:** This party says that graduate nurses are being trained here, but because of a lack of job openings, too many are being forced to look overseas instead of starting their careers in New Zealand. The pressure on the health system from the shortage of nurses spills over into patient healthcare.

**How:** This party would guarantee a job for every eligible New Zealand-trained nursing graduate, affecting about 2400 nurses. It would also address pressure on primary care because of the nursing shortage by doubling the funding available through the current recruitment subsidy. The current rate for rural nurses would be lifted from $20,000 to $40,000 and it would rise from $15,000 to $30,000 for nurses in urban areas. This party estimates that this policy would cost $525m.

**Costing (as stated):** This party estimates that this policy would cost $525m.

**Full text:** ['Labour will guarantee a job for graduate nurses', 31 August 2026 (accessed 01 September 2026)](documents/release-labour-will-guarantee-a-job-for-graduate-nurses.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/news/release-labour-will-guarantee-a-job-for-graduate-nurses/)); ['National moves the goalposts on jobs', 8 October 2026 (accessed 08 October 2026)](documents/release-national-moves-the-goalposts-on-jobs.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/news/release-national-moves-the-goalposts-on-jobs/)); [Graduate Nurse Job Guarantee](documents/graduate-nurse-job-guarantee.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/graduate-nurse-job-guarantee))

### Spend more on hospital maintenance and repairs

`POL55153` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Education, Transport & infrastructure

**Why:** This party says that NZ has a backlog of construction work. Homes need building, schools need improving and hospitals need fixing. Government investment will get this pipeline underway, helping to reduce high unemployment and opportunities for businesses to win work.

**How:** This party would tackle long-overdue repairs at hospitals so they are safe, reliable and fit for purpose. As part of this policy, more people will be helped into the trades by expanding the Apprenticeship Boost and Māori Trades Training scheme. This plan is costed at $200m.

### Free up more than 4.5 million GP appointments a year

`LAB-A01` · summary: *archive*

**Summary:** Labour says it would free up more than 4.5 million GP appointments a year through phone triage, better information for patients and technology that reduces paperwork (including AI scribes), backed by a new Digital Innovation Fund. ## Environment

### Provide loans for people to purchase solar set-ups for their homes

`POL54717` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Housing, Transport & infrastructure

**Why:** This party says that says that power bills have risen by 20 percent in the last two years. Solar power is the cheapest energy source available; however, high installation and equipment costs remain a large barrier for people. It says this policy would help people with these upfront costs, making cheap power accessible for all.

**How:** This party would create a SolarSaver fund, which includes two new Government-backed, long-term, low-interest finance options. The first loan is a Lines company loan, where you borrow through your local lines company to cover the cost of solar and a battery, repaid via your power bill. The second loan is a Ratepayer Assistance Scheme, a low-interest loan attached to your home covering solar, batteries and other home electrification. Repayments would be set below your power bill savings. A kickstart subsidy of up to $3,000 would be available for low- and middle-income households. The party would also amend power regulations so renters can use plug-in solar panels, with a subsidy available to cover the cost of purchase. Funding would come from the Government's Gas Security Fund. This party estimates that this policy would cost $160 million over four years.

**Costing (as stated):** This party estimates that this policy would cost $160 million over four years.

### Make Kiwisaver more flexible for workers

`POL54985` · summary: *policy.nz*

**Why:** This party says that Kiwisaver is crucial to building a secure future and a key source of investment for the economy. However, more than a million working-age KiwiSaver members are not contributing at all, while 83,400 are on a savings suspension. This party would take the government's proposed Kiwisaver plan and make it more flexible for workers, particularly those under financial pressure.

**How:** This party would make KiwiSaver more flexible and therefore more attractive for Kiwis to save. It would make employer contributions compulsory and lift them to 6 percent by 2032. It would extend employer contributions to workers over 65, and encompass the self-employed and those on parental leave. The default employee contribution would be set at 4 percent and the minimum contribution would be removed. Employer contributions would continue even when employees reduced or paused their own contributions. Contracts that absorb employer Kiwisaver contributions into total salaries would be banned.

### Introduce powers to protect consumers against price gouging

`POL55043` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Economy, Law, justice & government

**Why:** This party says that New Zealanders are paying too much for basic items such as food. It believes a crackdown is needed on big companies who charge excessive prices for essential goods or services. It notes that there is no legal test for excessive or unfair pricing in NZ.

**How:** This party would adjust legislation to address price gouging and give the Commerce Commission to new powers investigate what dominant companies are charging and take them to court. The legislation would only include industries that supply essentials such as food and groceries, banking and insurance, telecommunications, energy, fuel and investment. The law will apply where a company has enough market power that customers can't realistically switch, suppliers have nowhere else to go, or new competitors struggle to enter a market. Companies found to have overcharged consumers will face penalties and be ordered to make repayments. The policy would only touch big players with significant market powers, not small businesses.

`POL55312` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Education, Economy, Community & inclusion

**Why:** This party says that smart phones are one of the parenting challenges of our time. Tech companies have too much power over what we see and fake images are harder to spot. Many parents worry about what their children are seeing or if they are being bullied. More responsibility should be placed on the companies making money from these platforms.

**How:** This party would introduce more digital regulation to Parliament within the first 100 days, including no social media accounts for under-16s. Social media companies would be legally responsible for policing this, and a new digital duty of care will be introduced with stronger privacy and other protections for those under 18. Other action would include more control for users over their feeds, and stronger rules around deepfakes and non-consensual sexual images. An independent digital regulator will be created, with powers to take action against companies that break the rules.

**Full text:** ['Safer online' (PDF), 19 October 2026 (accessed 19 October 2026)](documents/safer-online.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/safer-online)); ['AI in New Zealand's interests', 9 September 2026 (accessed 09 September 2026)](documents/ai-for-new-zealand.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/ai-for-new-zealand)); ['Labour to make it safer for Kiwis online', 19 October 2026 (accessed 19 October 2026)](documents/release-labour-to-make-it-safer-for-kiwis-online.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/news/release-labour-to-make-it-safer-for-kiwis-online/)); ['Keeping kids off screens' (PDF), undated (accessed 19 October 2026)](documents/kids-off-screens.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/kids-off-screens)); ['Getting kids off screens and back to being kids', 18 October 2026 (accessed 19 October 2026)](documents/release-getting-kids-off-screens-and-back-to-being-kids.md) ([original](https://www.labour.org.nz/news/release-getting-kids-off-screens-and-back-to-being-kids/))

### Provide more support for children's sports and hobbies

`POL55313` · summary: *policy.nz* · also: Education, Economy, Community & inclusion

**Why:** This party says that parents and schools need help to keep kids safer online, keep them active and prevent screen addiction. Technology has its place, but at present it's a dominant force in children's lives while sport, hobbies and other after-school activities are out of reach for many families.

**How:** This party would boost funding for after school sport and activities with an extra $4m for Tū Manawa Active Aotearoa and $12m over four years for the Active Me - Kia Tū programme which supports families with sports registration, uniforms and equipment. This is part of a wider set of policies around AI and digital use which includes clear expectations around screentime in school and a continuation of the ban on mobile phones in class.
