# Andrew Little | | | |---|---| | **Party** | Labour | | **Status (Oct 2026)** | Former MP | | **Born** | 1965-05-07 — New Plymouth, New Zealand | | **Parliaments** | 50, 51, 52, 53 | | **First elected** | 2011 | | **Key roles** | 38th Mayor of Wellington (2025–)
35th Leader of the Opposition and 16th Leader of the Labour Party (2014–2017)
6th Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations (2017–2023)
42nd Minister of Health (2020–2023)
49th Minister of Justice (2017–2020)
33rd President of the Labour Party (2009–2011) | | **Wikipedia** | [Andrew Little (New Zealand politician)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Little_%28New_Zealand_politician%29) | ## Current status Little won the October 2025 Wellington mayoral election as Labour's endorsed candidate after incumbent Tory Whanau withdrew and endorsed him ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/559306/andrew-little-secures-labour-mayoral-nomination); [Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/nz-news/360851504/mayor-andrew-little-be-joined-wellington-city-council-ray-chung-no-place-tory-whanau)). As mayor he led a review and, in June 2026, a council vote to discontinue the $139m Golden Mile pedestrianisation project ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/598585/councillors-vote-against-continuing-wellington-s-golden-mile-project)), called for an inquiry into the Moa Point sewage plant failure, and declared a local state of emergency for heavy swells in June 2026. He resigned from Parliament on 5 December 2023 (Camilla Belich took his list seat) and is not a 2026 parliamentary candidate. He has publicly supported New Zealand's engagement with AUKUS, unlike Labour's current position ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/524955/former-defence-minister-andrew-little-disagrees-with-aukus-critics-on-china-threat)). ## Biography Born 7 May 1965 in New Plymouth, Little studied law, philosophy and public policy at Victoria University of Wellington and was VUWSA president (1987) and NZUSA president (1988–89). He became a lawyer for the Engineers' Union, its general counsel (1997) and national secretary of the EPMU, New Zealand's largest private-sector union, from 2000 to 2011; he was Labour Party president from 2009 to 2011 ([RNZ](http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/political/259657/little-takes-union-path-to-leadership)). He was successfully treated for prostate cancer in 2009 and lives in Island Bay with his wife Leigh and their son. ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 50th | 2011–2014 | List | 15 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | List | 11 | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | List | 3 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | List | 7 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 38th Mayor of Wellington | 17 October 2025 | present | | | 35th Leader of the Opposition and 16th Leader of the Labour Party | 18 November 2014 | 1 August 2017 | John Key; Bill English | | 6th Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations | 26 October 2017 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 42nd Minister of Health | 6 November 2020 | 1 February 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 49th Minister of Justice | 26 October 2017 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | | 33rd President of the Labour Party | 2 March 2009 | 2 April 2011 | | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - **List MP, 2011–2023.** Stood unsuccessfully in New Plymouth in 2011 and 2014; list-only thereafter. - **Labour leader and Leader of the Opposition, 18 Nov 2014 – 1 Aug 2017.** Narrowly beat Grant Robertson in the 2014 leadership election, carried by the union affiliates' vote ([Stuff](http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/63305825/Andrew-Little-new-Labour-Party-leader-by-a-whisker)). Credited with ending caucus infighting but polled poorly; he resigned seven weeks before the 2017 election, handing over to Jacinda Ardern — a move later widely described as selfless ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=11935044)). - **Minister, 2017–2023 (12 portfolios):** Justice and Courts (2017–2020), Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations (2017–2023), GCSB and NZSIS (2017–2023), Pike River Re-entry, Workplace Relations (2020), Health (Nov 2020 – Jan 2023), Defence and Public Service (2023), Immigration (June 2023), and lead coordination minister for the Christchurch mosque attack Royal Commission response ([Parliament profile](https://www.parliament.nz/en/mps-and-electorates/former-members-of-parliament/little-andrew/)). ## Record & notable actions - **Abortion law reform:** as Justice Minister he introduced the bill that removed abortion from the Crimes Act; it passed as the Abortion Legislation Act 2020 ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/120389800/new-zealands-fourdecade-old-abortion-laws-have-changed-after-law-passes-final-reading)). - **Pike River:** established the Pike River Recovery Agency and in 2018 entered the portal with families; the drift was re-entered in 2019, but plans to recover the miners' remains were abandoned in 2021 ([Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/andrew-little-enters-pike-river-portal)). - **Health:** as Health Minister (2020–2023) he oversaw the health system through the COVID-19 period; in mid-2022 he said the system was under pressure but not in crisis, which health workers disputed ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/469518/health-system-under-pressure-not-in-crisis-minister-andrew-little)). - **Three strikes:** his 2018 plan to repeal the three-strikes law was blocked by NZ First ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12068425)). - **Intelligence:** in July 2021 publicly attributed malicious cyber activity to Chinese state-sponsored actor APT40 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/447239/government-points-finger-at-china-over-cyber-attacks)). - **Treaty settlements:** delivered Crown apologies including to Ngāti Maru (Taranaki) in 2022. - **Opposition:** drafted a corporate manslaughter member's bill after Pike River and the CTV collapse (2013). ## Controversies - **Defamation suits:** ACC Minister Judith Collins sued Little and Trevor Mallard for defamation in 2012 (settled); in 2017 hotel owners Earl and Lani Hagaman sued him over remarks linking their National Party donation to a government contract — the jury cleared him on some claims and could not agree on others, and no damages were awarded ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10847321); [RNZ](http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/national/328552/little-%27very-pleased%27-no-damages-awarded)). - **Australian deportations (2018):** a public dispute with Australian ministers Peter Dutton and Alex Hawke after he criticised Australia's "501" deportation policy ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12092448)). ## 2026 candidacy Not listed as a Labour candidate for the 2026 election on policy.nz (Oct 2026). ## Sources - She was an infectious-diseases physician at Capital & Coast DHB, a senior lecturer at the University of Otago, Wellington, and an elected (Labour) member and deputy chair of the Capital & Coast DHB from 2019 ([Otago profile](https://www.otago.ac.nz/healthsciences/expertise/Profile/index.html?id=1377)). In April 2020 her independent audit of COVID-19 contact tracing found the system under-staffed and slow to scale; the Ministry of Health accepted her recommendations ([Ministry of Health](https://www.health.govt.nz/publication/rapid-audit-contact-tracing-covid-19-new-zealand)). Re-elected on the list in 2023. - **Minister, 2020–2023:** Minister for Seniors and Food Safety and Associate Minister of Health and of Research, Science and Innovation (Nov 2020); Minister for COVID-19 Response and Research, Science and Innovation (June 2022); Minister of Health (Feb–Nov 2023), saying her priorities were "workforce, wait lists and winter" ([The Post](https://www.thepost.co.nz/politics/360540648/its-worst-job-country-why-does-ayesha-verrall-want-second-go-it)). - **Opposition:** health, public service and Wellington issues spokesperson (Nov 2023); kept health and Wellington after March 2025. ## Record & notable actions - **Smokefree Generation law:** as associate health minister she led the Smokefree 2025 plan and the 2022 law banning tobacco sales to anyone born on or after 1 January 2009, cutting nicotine levels and retail outlets ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/dec/13/new-zealand-passes-world-first-tobacco-law-to-ban-smoking-by-2025)). An employment lawyer (LLB(Hons) Victoria, MJur Auckland), he was a partner in Minter Ellison Rudd Watts, chaired the NZ AIDS Foundation and was deputy chair of Meridian Energy and the Lotteries Commission. ## Political career ### Career summary - **List MP 2006–2013**, entering on Jim Sutton's retirement ([Scoop](http://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA0607/S00121.htm)); lost to Peter Dunne in Ōhariu-Belmont/Ōhariu in 2005, 2008 and 2011. - Chaired the Finance and Expenditure Committee (2007–2008); Labour spokesperson for energy, climate change and environment (2008–2011), then justice and arts and shadow attorney-general (2011–2013). ## Record & notable actions - Drafted a member's bill (2009) to repeal the provocation defence to murder; a Government bill achieving this passed 116–5 in November 2009 ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=10612028&pnum=1)). - Member of the UN Global Commission on HIV and the Law (2010). ## Controversies - His 2007 appointment as a parliamentary private secretary was delayed after he announced it before it was confirmed, angering Prime Minister Helen Clark ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/733/Ambitious-Chauvel-angers-PM-in-reshuffle)). ## 2026 candidacy Not listed as a Labour candidate for the 2026 election on policy.nz (Oct 2026). ## Sources - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Chauvel - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Chauvel_%28politician%29 - https://www.thepost.co.nz/nz-news/350156526/life-after-politics-finding-new-buzz-beyond-beehive - http://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA0607/S00121.htm - http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=10612028&pnum=1 - https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/733/Ambitious-Chauvel-angers-PM-in-reshuffle _Profile compiled 2026-10-23 from the sources above; Wikipedia tables parsed by tools/people_labour_build.py._

# Chris Hipkins | | | |---|---| | **Party** | Labour | | **Status (Oct 2026)** | Current MP, standing in 2026 | | **Born** | 1978-09-05 — Hutt Valley, New Zealand | | **Electorate(s) held** | Rimutaka, Remutaka | | **Parliaments** | 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54 | | **First elected** | 2008 | | **2026 candidacy** | Remutaka · list #1 | | **Key roles** | Labour shadow cabinet #1 (as of 11 Mar 2026): Leader of the Opposition; Spokesperson for Ministerial Services; Spokesperson for National Security and Intelligence
41st Leader of the Opposition (2023–)
41st Prime Minister of New Zealand (2023)
18th Leader of the Labour Party (2023–)
Minister of National Security and Intelligence (2023)
Leader of the House (2017–2023) | | **Wikipedia** | [Chris Hipkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Hipkins) | ## Current status Hipkins is Leader of the Opposition and Labour leader heading into the 7 November 2026 general election, in which he is standing again in Remutaka and is first on Labour's list ([policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party)). Labour's caucus confirmed him as leader after the 2023 defeat on 7 November 2023 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/501872/labour-votes-to-keep-chris-hipkins-as-leader-carmel-sepuloni-takes-over-as-deputy)). In October 2025 he announced that Labour would campaign on a narrow 28% capital gains tax on property sales (excluding the family home and farms) to fund three free doctor's visits a year, and ruled out a wealth tax ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/577021/labour-to-campaign-on-narrow-capital-gains-tax-no-wealth-tax)). ## Biography Christopher John Hipkins was born on 5 September 1978 in the Hutt Valley, the son of Doug and Rosemary Hipkins ([Parliament maiden statement](https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/hansard-debates/rhr/document/49HansS_20081216_00001004/hipkins-chris-maiden-statements); [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/482831/chris-hipkins-from-head-boy-to-prime-minister)). He was head boy of Hutt Valley Memorial College in 1996 and studied political science and criminology at Victoria University of Wellington (BA), where he was students' association president in 2000 and 2001 ([Beehive biography](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/minister/biography/chris-hipkins)). As a first-year student in 1997 he was among protesters arrested at Parliament over the Tertiary Review green paper; a decade later the protesters received an apology and compensation after a court found the arrests unjustified ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/dominion-post/news/local-papers/hutt-news/2595536/Parliament-to-say-sorry-to-protestors)). Before entering Parliament he was a policy adviser at the Industry Training Federation, a training manager at Todd Energy, and an adviser to ministers Trevor Mallard and Prime Minister Helen Clark ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/chris-hipkins-from-hutt-valley-boy-to-quiet-coup-for-pm-audrey-young-reports/ET4JZSI5PVCKBDDHRCLYVQ3CHI/)). He married Jade in 2020; they separated in 2022 and have two children. In 2018 he took extended paternity leave, one of the first senior male cabinet ministers to do so. His relationship with Toni Grace became public on election night 2023 and he announced their engagement in November 2025 ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/labour-leader-chris-hipkins-reveals-engagement-to-partner-toni-grace/32RDT6TDINBDBCJ3XR2Z23OIAQ/)). ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 49th | 2008–2011 | Rimutaka | 47 | Labour | | 50th | 2011–2014 | Rimutaka | 30 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | Rimutaka | 9 | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Rimutaka | 7 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Remutaka | 6 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–present | Remutaka | 1 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 41st Leader of the Opposition | 27 November 2023 | present | Christopher Luxon | | 41st Prime Minister of New Zealand | 25 January 2023 | 27 November 2023 | | | 18th Leader of the Labour Party | 22 January 2023 | present | | | Minister of National Security and Intelligence | 25 January 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Himself | | Leader of the House | 26 October 2017 | 25 January 2023 | Jacinda Ardern | | Minister of Education | 26 October 2017 | 25 January 2023 | Jacinda Ardern | | Minister of Public Service | 26 October 2017 | 25 January 2023 | Jacinda Ardern | | Minister of Police | 14 June 2022 | 25 January 2023 | Jacinda Ardern | | Minister for COVID-19 Response | 6 November 2020 | 14 June 2022 | Jacinda Ardern | | Minister of Health | 2 July 2020 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Opposition portfolios (as of 11 March 2026) Rank 1 in Chris Hipkins' shadow cabinet: - Leader of the Opposition - Spokesperson for Ministerial Services - Spokesperson for National Security and Intelligence _Source: [Shadow Cabinet of Chris Hipkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Cabinet_of_Chris_Hipkins), list as of 11 March 2026._ ### Career summary **Electorate.** Hipkins won the Labour-held Rimutaka seat (renamed Remutaka in 2020) in 2008 after Paul Swain retired, beating union official Paul Chalmers for the nomination. His majorities: 753 (2008), 3,286 (2011), 6,664 (2014), 8,609 (2017), 8,859 (2023); in 2020 he polled 20,497 votes (official results via [electionresults.govt.nz 2011](http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2011/electorate-43.html), [2014](http://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2014/electorate-44.html), [2017](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/electorate-details-44.html), [2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-42.html), [2023](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-42.html)). **Opposition, 2008–2017.** Spokesperson for internal affairs in his first term; under David Shearer he entered the shadow cabinet as education and state services spokesperson and became Labour's chief whip; he kept education under David Cunliffe, Andrew Little and Jacinda Ardern and was also shadow Leader of the House from 2014 ([Parliament profile](https://www.parliament.nz/en/mps-and-electorates/members-of-parliament/hipkins-chris/)). **Minister, 2017–2023.** In the Sixth Labour Government he was Minister of Education and Leader of the House (26 Oct 2017 – 25 Jan 2023), Minister for the Public Service (2017–2023), Minister of Health (2 Jul – 6 Nov 2020, after David Clark resigned), Minister for COVID-19 Response (6 Nov 2020 – 14 Jun 2022) and Minister of Police (14 Jun 2022 – 25 Jan 2023), earning a reputation as the government's "fixer" ([The Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/21-01-2023/the-guy-just-lives-for-diy-what-to-expect-from-prime-minister-chris-hipkins); [DPMC ministerial list Nov 2020](https://dpmc.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2020-11/ministerial-list-2-nov-2020.pdf)). **Prime Minister, 2023.** After Jacinda Ardern resigned, Hipkins was the only nominee for the Labour leadership (21–22 January 2023) and was sworn in as the 41st Prime Minister on 25 January 2023, with Carmel Sepuloni as the first Pasifika deputy prime minister ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/chris-hipkins-sworn-in-as-prime-minister-carmel-sepuloni-as-deputy-jacinda-ardern-vacates-top-job/IERZGZV2BFAE5AWLNJHMMGHYQ4/)). He led Labour to defeat at the October 2023 election (26.91% of the party vote, 34 seats) and conceded on election night ([Electoral Commission](https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2023/official-results-for-the-2023-general-election/); [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/500185/election-2023-labour-s-chris-hipkins-concedes-congratulates-national-on-results)). He remained caretaker PM until Christopher Luxon was sworn in on 27 November 2023. **Opposition leader, 2023–present.** He took the ministerial services and national security & intelligence spokesperson roles in his shadow cabinet ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/503581/labour-party-leader-chris-hipkins-reveals-new-shadow-cabinet)) and in March 2025 reshuffled it and created an economic team led by Barbara Edmonds ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/544048/chris-hipkins-announces-new-labour-economic-team-tangi-utikere-promoted)). ## Record & notable actions - **Education (2017–2023):** legislated to stop new charter schools; all 12 existing charter schools became state-integrated or special-character schools by September 2018 ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2018/09/all-nz-charter-schools-now-approved-to-become-state-integrated.html)). Abolished National Standards and reviewed NCEA. Merged the 16 polytechnics and the industry training organisations into Te Pūkenga (from April 2020), a reform that by 2022 faced low enrolments, deficits and senior resignations ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/395722/government-confirms-major-overhaul-of-polytechnics-apprenticeships); [Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/waikato-times/300647698/minister-rules-out-te-pkenga-commissioner-at-this-time)). Declined Victoria University's proposed renaming to "University of Wellington" in 2018 ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/education/109441495/victoria-university-of-wellington-name-change-rejected-by-minister)). - **COVID-19 response (2020–2022):** introduced mask mandates on public transport, pre-departure testing, the My Vaccine Pass and the COVID-19 Response (Vaccinations) Legislation Act 2021 (vaccine-mandate framework) ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/456455/mandate-legislation-pushed-through-parliament-amid-fierce-opposition)); oversaw MIQ, including the January 2022 pause of the MIQ lottery ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/459786/government-postpones-next-miq-lottery-due-to-spike-of-omicron-cases-at-border)); announced in October 2022 the end of most COVID powers and a Royal Commission of Inquiry ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/476919/government-signals-covid-19-inquiry-in-the-works)). - **As Prime Minister (2023):** a "policy bonfire" scrapping or deferring the TVNZ–RNZ merger, the biofuel mandate, lowering the voting age to 16, the Clean Car Upgrade and much of the speed-reduction programme, and delaying social insurance and hate-speech law, with funds redirected to cost-of-living support ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/483875/watch-tvnz-rnz-merger-scrapped-income-insurance-and-hate-speech-laws-delayed); [1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/03/13/pms-policy-bonfire-voting-age-bill-transport-schemes-reprioritsed/)); led the response to the Auckland Anniversary floods and Cyclone Gabrielle; Budget 2023 removed $5 prescription fees, extended 20 hours ECE to two-year-olds and made public transport free for under-13s ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/490161/budget-2023-at-a-glance-what-you-need-to-know)); signed the NZ–EU free trade agreement on 9 July 2023 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/493457/new-zealand-signs-free-trade-deal-with-european-union-after-years-of-negotiations)); ruled out a capital gains or wealth tax for the 2023 term ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/493596/hipkins-rules-out-capital-gains-tax-wealth-tax-if-labour-re-elected)). - **In opposition:** called for a Gaza ceasefire (November 2023) and in September 2025 said New Zealand should recognise the situation in Gaza as genocide ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/573334/nz-govt-will-not-respond-on-latest-accusation-of-genocide-in-gaza)); in April 2026 committed Labour's votes to pass the NZ–India free trade agreement, which NZ First opposed ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/business/593185/chris-hipkins-announces-labour-will-back-india-free-trade-deal)). - **Conscience votes:** voted for the Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill in 2013 ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/gay-marriage-how-mps-voted/WLPKK4734FBZEKJIDHBFO4MWFA/)). - **Member's bills:** Electricity (Renewable Preference) Amendment Bill (defeated at first reading, 2010); Education (Charter Schools Abolition) Amendment Bill (defeated at first reading, 2016) ([Parliament](https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/bills-and-laws/bills-proposed-laws/document/00DBHOH_BILL68842_1/education-charter-schools-abolition-amendment-bill)). ## Controversies - **Charlotte Bellis MIQ case (2022):** as COVID-19 Response Minister he publicly released details about pregnant journalist Charlotte Bellis's emergency MIQ application; she said she had not consented and disputed his account. In June 2022 he formally apologised for releasing personal information without consent and for inaccurate comments ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/covid-19-omicron-chris-hipkins-formally-apologises-over-charlotte-bellis-emergency-miq-saga/DX35AVZARU5RPUFTFUKDCNMK5A/)). - **Remarks about Bill English (2022):** apologised to former PM Bill English after suggesting in the House that English had favoured his brothers with government contracts ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/129959240/chris-hipkins-apologises-to-bill-english-for-dragging-family-into-debate)). - **As PM he dealt with several ministerial resignations/dismissals** — Stuart Nash, Meka Whaitiri, Michael Wood, Kiri Allan and Jan Tinetti's referral to the Privileges Committee (see those profiles). - **COVID vaccine advice for under-18s (2026):** the NZ Herald reported he had been briefed in March 2022 on advice to reduce the second-dose mandate for 12–17-year-olds; he initially denied receiving the Cabinet paper then said he had forgotten, and rejected Winston Peters' claim that he misled the COVID-19 Royal Commission ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/the-covid-vaccine-and-the-risk-to-under-18s-chris-hipkins-defends-not-making-advice-public/W3RWZP2RLVGLFJA3EUGNM62GDI/); [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/590823/labour-leader-chris-hipkins-denies-misleading-public-over-covid-vaccine-risk-to-under-18s)). ## 2026 candidacy - # Clare Curran | | | |---|---| | **Party** | Labour | | **Status (Oct 2026)** | Former MP | | **Born** | 1960 — Lower Hutt, New Zealand | | **Electorate(s) held** | Dunedin South | | **Parliaments** | 49, 50, 51, 52 | | **First elected** | 2008 | | **Key roles** | 25th Minister of Broadcasting, Communications and Digital Media (2017–2018)
Minister for Government Digital Services (2017–2018) | | **Wikipedia** | [Clare Curran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clare_Curran) | ## Current status Curran left Parliament in 2020. She has served on the University of Otago Council and the board of Network for Learning, chairs the Dunedin Night Shelter Trust, and has been chair and later co-general manager of Life Matters Suicide Prevention Trust; she has also been writing a crime novel ([The Post](https://www.thepost.co.nz/nz-news/350156526/life-after-politics-finding-new-buzz-beyond-beehive); [ODT](https://www.odt.co.nz/news/dunedin/health/curran-takes-hands-role-life-matters)). ## Biography Born in 1960 and raised in Dunedin, Curran holds a BA from Otago and BA (Hons) in anthropology from Victoria. **Foreign-buyer ban:** led the Overseas Investment Amendment Act 2018 banning most foreign purchases of existing homes ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2018/aug/15/tenants-on-our-own-land-new-zealand-bans-sale-of-homes-to-foreign-buyers)). - **Trade:** signed the CPTPP (March 2018), led ratification of PACER Plus, launched UK FTA talks, and cancelled the Saudi "sheep deal" he had exposed in opposition ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/government-axes-saudi-sheep-deal/7KXXQSKRAU26OR2A737MPGM2TY/)). - **Resource management:** replaced the RMA with the Natural and Built Environment Act 2023 and Spatial Planning Act 2023 (passed 16 August 2023; repealed by the next government in December 2023) ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/government-passes-rma-replacement-bills-ending-30-years-of-rma/EUKOHYGWNNA3TDZYQYRI64446U/)); Essential Freshwater rules including winter-grazing controls (2020), criticised by farm lobbies as unworkable and by some scientists as too weak. - **Emissions Trading Scheme:** as climate change minister in 2008 he legislated the NZ ETS ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/climate-change-bill-becomes-law/BXWMGB3XSP4X6BJHJECTRAFI54/)). - **Attorney-General:** steered the COVID-19 Public Health Response Act 2020 (the High Court later found the first nine days of the 2020 lockdown, while justified, were not lawful) ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/423917/high-court-rules-some-of-covid-19-level-4-lockdown-was-unlawful)); oversaw the appointment of Helen Winkelmann as Chief Justice and of Joe Williams, the first Māori Supreme Court judge; passed the Bill of Rights (Declarations of Inconsistency) Amendment Act 2022. - **Tax fairness:** commissioned IRD research (2023) finding the wealthiest families paid a lower effective tax rate than most New Zealanders ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/488705/wealthiest-paying-tax-at-much-lower-rate-than-most-other-new-zealanders-ird-report)); passed the Tax Principles Reporting Act 2023, repealed under urgency in December 2023 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/505298/parliament-repeals-tax-principles-reporting-law-under-urgency)). - **Conscience votes:** for civil unions (2004), marriage equality (2013), and the End of Life Choice Act (2019); against the 2003 euthanasia bill. ## Controversies - **2006 resignation:** resigned as Attorney-General and from Cabinet after a former business partner alleged he filed an incorrect Companies Office declaration; the Companies Office cleared him and he was reappointed ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/parker-heads-back-into-the-cabinet/G5FSJ3CZB4UEZG7X4VFSGOKBJA/)). - **Clare Curran hiring (2007):** the State Services Commission cleared him of improper pressure in suggesting the environment ministry hire Labour activist Clare Curran, though critics disputed the finding ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/no-ministerial-pressure-in-curran-job-report/LXTB3L3NSF3CFOBVXXP6DMOXKY/)). - **GST on KiwiSaver fees (2022):** a proposal to apply GST to KiwiSaver fees was dropped after a backlash; the 2022 cost-of-living payment was also criticised for paying people who were not eligible ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/473822/government-drops-plans-to-charge-gst-on-kiwisaver-fees)). - **Resignation as revenue minister (July 2023):** quit the portfolio, calling it "untenable" after Hipkins ruled out his wealth/capital gains tax work; some commentators called the timing petulant, others principled ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/132611615/david-parker-untenable-to-remain-revenue-minister-after-wealth-tax-rejection); [NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/claire-trevett-david-parkers-ill-timed-bout-of-principle-on-taxes-delivers-a-headache-for-chris-hipkins/2R5I3YCCKJEM3JLBMLI3STGFEU/)). - **EPA chair dismissal (2023):** removed Rob Campbell as Environmental Protection Authority chair after Campbell publicly criticised National's Three Waters stance in breach of neutrality expectations ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/485149/ousted-health-boss-rob-campbell-also-dumped-as-chair-of-epa)). ## 2026 candidacy Not listed as a Labour candidate for the 2026 election on policy.nz (Oct 2026). ## Sources - 15th Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs (2023) | | **Wikipedia** | [Duncan Webb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_Webb) | ## Current status Webb announced on 21 October 2025 that he would not seek re-election ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/labour-mp-duncan-webb-to-resign-as-mp-wont-seek-re-election/XALPZELGH5DZDJK46P5UI2D7JY/)); he stood down as Deputy Shadow Leader of the House in March 2026 and holds no portfolio in the final shadow cabinet list. In November 2025 he lodged a member's bill to repeal the Regulatory Standards Act 2025, which Labour promises to repeal within 100 days ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/579942/labour-lodges-member-s-bill-to-repeal-regulatory-standards-act-asks-nz-first-for-support)). In June 2026 China banned him and three other MPs from China, Hong Kong and Macau for a year after a cross-party visit to Taiwan; Webb said he would "pay that price" ([AP](https://apnews.com/article/new-zealand-china-mps-banned-taiwan-beijing-3b2745d7fe9e9db7f26b56187d82b07e)). ## Biography Born in 1967 in London and raised in Christchurch from age six, Webb studied law at Canterbury (LLB Hons 1989; LLD 2007), lectured at Massey and Victoria, was a law professor at Canterbury (2000–2008) and then a partner at Lane Neave. He worked with the Public Interest Project and the Howard League ([Scoop](http://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/AK1605/S00057/duncan-webb-nominated-for-christchurch-central.htm)). He has three sons. ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Christchurch Central | 43 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Christchurch Central | 43 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–present | Christchurch Central | 20 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 17th Minister for State Owned Enterprises | 1 February 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 15th Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs | 1 February 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - **Christchurch Central MP 2017–2026:** won the seat from National's Nicky Wagner (majority 2,871), then 14,098 (2020) and 1,841 (2023) ([2017](http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/electorate-details-04.html); Member of the New Zealand Parliament (2017–) | | **Wikipedia** | [Ginny Andersen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ginny_Andersen) | ## Current status Andersen is No. 9 in Labour's shadow cabinet; she took education in the 11 March 2026 reshuffle alongside police, jobs and income and Treaty negotiations ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360949687/hipkins-reshuffles-labour-portfolios-henare-departs-and-plan-hatched-maori-seats-race)). In April 2026 she announced Labour would restore school boards' Treaty of Waitangi obligations and reverse several of the coalition's curriculum and testing changes ([Newsroom](https://newsroom.co.nz/2026/04/28/labour-vows-to-reinstate-school-boards-treaty-obligations/)). She is contesting Hutt South again (list No. 12) ([policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party)). On 15 September 2026 the Speaker ordered her out of the chamber for heckling ([Newstalk ZB](https://www.newstalkzb.co.nz/news/politics/speaker-gerry-brownlee-boots-two-mps-from-house-within-minutes/)). ## Biography Born in 1975 and raised around New Zealand by teacher parents before settling in Christchurch (Avonside Girls' High), Andersen studied political science and te reo Māori at the University of Canterbury (MA 2004, on the Ngāi Tahu settlement). She worked at the Office of Treaty Settlements, as private secretary to Margaret Wilson and adviser to David Cunliffe and Trevor Mallard, then for New Zealand Police (from 2006) as a policy manager on gangs and organised crime, including secondment to DPMC on the Methamphetamine Action Plan ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/03/20/minister-of-police-who-is-ginny-andersen/)). She was Labour Party vice-president from 2015. She is married to former police inspector Geoff Gwyn. ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 52nd | 2017–2020 | List | 28 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Hutt South | 45 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–present | List | 17 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 52nd Minister of Justice | 24 July 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 42nd Minister of Police | 20 March 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 2nd Minister for the Digital Economy and Communications | 1 February 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 14th Minister for Seniors | 1 February 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | Member of the New Zealand Parliament | 23 September 2017 | present | | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Opposition portfolios (as of 11 March 2026) Rank 9 in Chris Hipkins' shadow cabinet: - Spokesperson for Education - Spokesperson for Police - Spokesperson for Jobs and Income - Spokesperson for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations _Source: [Shadow Cabinet of Chris Hipkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Cabinet_of_Chris_Hipkins), list as of 11 March 2026._ ### Career summary - Lost Ōhāriu to Peter Dunne by 710 votes in 2014; lost Hutt South to Chris Bishop in 2017 (entering on the list); won Hutt South from Bishop by 3,777 in 2020; lost it back to Bishop by 1,332 in 2023 and returned on the list ([2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-14.html); [2023](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-14.html)). - Chair of the Justice Committee (2020–2023). - **Minister, 2023:** entered Cabinet on 31 January 2023 (Digital Economy and Communications, Small Business, Seniors); Minister of Police from 20 March 2023 after Stuart Nash's removal; Minister of Justice from July 2023 after Kiri Allan's resignation ([The Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/live-updates/20-03-2023/junior-minister-ginny-anderson-takes-over-police-role-from-stuart-nash)). ## Record & notable actions - **Miscarriage bereavement leave:** her member's bill, giving three days' paid bereavement leave after miscarriage or stillbirth, passed unanimously in March 2021 — one of the first such laws in the world ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/439076/miscarriage-bereavement-leave-bill-passes-unanimously-in-parliament)). - As Police Minister introduced a specific ram-raid offence and oversaw fleeing-driver legislation and fog-cannon subsidies for small retailers ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/496851/bill-targeting-ram-raid-offending-passes-first-reading)). ## Controversies - **Hutt South office sublease (2020):** a decades-old arrangement inherited from Trevor Mallard saw Parliamentary Service pay Labour more rent than Labour paid the landlord, with the difference used by the party; she ended it once it became public ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300098040/taxpayer-foots-bill-for-labour-electorate-funds-in-decadesold-subletting-arrangement)). - **Volunteer bullying complaints (Nov 2023):** Labour investigated a complaint that she had berated a teenage volunteer on election night; she apologised. A second volunteer's allegations she disputed ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/502320/labour-mp-ginny-andersen-formally-apologises-after-bullying-accusation)). - **Mark Mitchell remarks (Feb 2024):** asked whether Police Minister Mark Mitchell had been "paid to kill people" as a private security contractor in Iraq; after Hipkins disagreed, she said her comments "went too far" and apologised ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/labours-ginny-andersen-claims-police-minister-was-paid-to-kill-people-while-working-in-private-security-overseas/RB62YR5I3BEDZLU7JYOM27OKDU/)). - 12th Leader of the House (2023) | | **Wikipedia** | [Grant Robertson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Robertson) | ## Current status Robertson resigned from Parliament on 22 March 2024 and has been Vice-Chancellor of the University of Otago since 1 July 2024 ([University of Otago](https://www.otago.ac.nz/news/newsroom/university-of-otago-announces-appointment-of-new-vice-chancellor)); Glen Bennett replaced him as a list MP. His appointment drew a mixed response, with some donors and alumni objecting to a former politician without an academic background ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/nz-news/350251587/shame-you-emails-show-not-everyone-happy-grant-robertsons-appointment-otago-unis)). In August 2025 he apologised for how cuts to Otago's doctoral scholarships were communicated ([ODT](https://www.odt.co.nz/news/dunedin/robertson-sorry-way-slashed-scholarships-communicated)), and in March 2026 announced a new Otago campus in Queenstown ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/588625/university-of-otago-to-offer-new-qualifications-in-queenstown-as-part-of-campus-plans)). He is not a 2026 candidate. ## Biography Grant Murray Robertson was born on 30 October 1971 in Palmerston North and grew up in South Dunedin, where he was head boy of King's High School. He graduated BA (Hons) in political studies from the University of Otago (1995), was Otago University Students' Association president (1993) and co-president of the national students' association (1996) ([NZ Listener](http://www.listener.co.nz/current-affairs/politics/interview-labour-deputy-grant-robertson/)). He was a diplomat with MFAT from 1997 to 2001 (including a UN posting and managing the Samoa aid programme), then an adviser to minister Marian Hobbs and to Prime Minister Helen Clark, and later worked for the University of Otago in Wellington. He lives in Wellington with his partner Alf Kaiwai (civil union 2009) and was New Zealand's first openly gay deputy prime minister ([AP](https://apnews.com/article/cabinets-grant-robertson-new-zealand-c840239beabda3fd6f3fbdd81fd5ea4f)). ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 49th | 2008–2011 | Wellington Central | 46 | Labour | | 50th | 2011–2014 | Wellington Central | 14 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | Wellington Central | 3 | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Wellington Central | 4 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Wellington Central | 3 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–2024 | List | 4 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 10th Vice-Chancellor of the University of Otago | 1 July 2024 | present | | | 19th Deputy Prime Minister of New Zealand | 6 November 2020 | 25 January 2023 | Jacinda Ardern | | 29th Minister of Foreign Affairs | 11 November 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 12th Minister of Disarmament and Arms Control | 11 November 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 42nd Minister of Finance | 26 October 2017 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 12th Leader of the House | 1 February 2023 | 27 November 2023 ; Acting: 25 January 2023 – 1 February 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 11th Minister for Sport and Recreation | 26 October 2017 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 4th Minister for Infrastructure | 6 November 2020 | 1 February 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 13th Minister for Racing | 6 November 2020 | 14 June 2022 | Jacinda Ardern | | 19th Minister Responsible for the Earthquake Commission | 27 June 2019 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | | Deputy Leader of the Opposition | 13 December 2011 | 17 September 2013 | | | Deputy Leader of the Labour Party | 13 December 2011 | 17 September 2013 | | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - **Wellington Central, 2008–2023.** Won the seat in 2008 (majority 1,904 over Stephen Franks), then held it with majorities of 6,376 (2011), 8,267 (2014), 9,963 (2017, over Nicola Willis) and 18,878 (2020, over Willis) ([2008](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2008/electorate-59.html), [2011](http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2011/electorate-59.html), [2014](https://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2014/electorate-60.html), [2017](https://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/electorate-details-60.html), [2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-60.html)). In 2023 he stood list-only and returned as a list MP ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/483193/grant-robertson-goes-list-only-will-not-contest-wellington-central)). - **Opposition, 2008–2017.** Spokesperson for state services, tertiary education and (from 2011) health; deputy leader under David Shearer (13 Dec 2011 – 17 Sep 2013). Ran for leader in 2013 (won most caucus votes but lost to David Cunliffe on members' and affiliates' votes) and 2014 (lost to Andrew Little 50.52%–49.48% after preferences) ([Stuff 2013](http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/9166765/Cunliffe-wins-Labour-leadership); [Stuff 2014](http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/63305825/Andrew-Little-new-Labour-Party-leader-by-a-whisker)). Finance spokesperson from November 2014; chaired Labour's Future of Work Commission (report 2016). - **Minister of Finance, 26 Oct 2017 – 27 Nov 2023,** throughout the Ardern and Hipkins governments; also Minister for Sport and Recreation (2017–2023), Earthquake Commission (2019–2020), Infrastructure (2020–2023), Racing (2020–2022), Deputy Prime Minister (6 Nov 2020 – 25 Jan 2023, after Kelvin Davis declined the role), Leader of the House and Minister for Cyclone Recovery under Hipkins (2023), and briefly Minister of Foreign Affairs in the caretaker period (Nov 2023) ([DPMC ministerial list 2020](https://dpmc.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2020-11/ministerial-list-2-nov-2020.pdf); [Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/131290992/pm-chris-hipkins-announces-ministers-to-lead-regional-cyclone-recovery-efforts)). - **After January 2023:** declined to seek the leadership when Ardern resigned ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/01/19/grant-robertson-says-he-will-not-stand-as-next-labour-leader/)). Finance and racing spokesperson in opposition until he announced his retirement on 20 February 2024. ## Record & notable actions - Delivered six Budgets (2018–2023) as finance minister, including the pandemic-era budgets; he was the government's lead on the economic response to COVID-19 and often deputised for Ardern at pandemic briefings ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/opinion/123133786/election-2020-why-kelvin-davis-will-probably-be-the-next-deputy-prime-minister)). - Member's bill: Ethical Investment (Crown Financial Institutions) Bill (2010), defeated at first reading ([RNZ](http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/stories/2010/08/05/d20e2514bc14)). - Retained the title "The Honourable" on retirement from the Executive Council (December 2023) ([NZ Gazette](https://gazette.govt.nz/notice/id/2023-vr5732)). ## Controversies - In February 2021 he withdrew from a weekly slot on Magic Talk after host Peter Williams asked him about the World Economic Forum's "Great Reset", saying he did not want to keep shooting down conspiracy theories ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/entertainment/tv-radio/124301816/grant-robertson-axes-weekly-interview-on-magic-talk-radio-show)). - His record as Finance Minister divides opinion: commentator Morgan Godfery called him a top-performing minister ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/opinion/130872334/morgan-godfery-topperforming-minister-but-you-wouldnt-know-it)), while some Otago donors and alumni cited that record when objecting to his appointment as vice-chancellor ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/nz-news/350251587/shame-you-emails-show-not-everyone-happy-grant-robertsons-appointment-otago-unis)). ## 2026 candidacy Not listed as a Labour candidate for the 2026 election on policy.nz (Oct 2026). ## Sources - Member of the New Zealand Parliament (2008–2023) | | **Wikipedia** | [Jacinda Ardern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacinda_Ardern) | ## Current status Dame Jacinda Ardern left Parliament at the 2023 election and is not involved in the 2026 campaign as a candidate. After office she took up dual fellowships at the Harvard Kennedy School (2023) ([AP](https://apnews.com/article/new-zealand-jacinda-ardern-harvard-university-d9d82f742e79815e91687bd54213bd53)), became a trustee of Prince William's Earthshot Prize ([BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-65180096)), was appointed Special Envoy for the Christchurch Call by Chris Hipkins in April 2023 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/487340/former-pm-jacinda-ardern-appointed-as-christchurch-call-envoy)), and published her memoir *A Different Kind of Power* in June 2025, which won the 2026 E. H. McCormick Prize for best first book of general non-fiction ([NZ Book Awards](https://www.nzbookawards.nz/new-zealand-book-awards/2026-awards/winners/)). In February 2026 *The Guardian* reported that she and her family had moved to Sydney ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/feb/26/jacinda-ardern-living-in-australia-former-nz-new-zealand-pm)). She was made a Dame Grand Companion of the New Zealand Order of Merit in 2023 ([DPMC](https://www.dpmc.govt.nz/publications/kings-birthday-and-coronation-honours-list-2023)). ## Biography Born 26 July 1980 in Hamilton and raised in Morrinsville and Murupara (her father was a police officer), Ardern joined Labour at 17 and graduated from the University of Waikato with a Bachelor of Communication Studies in 2001 ([Waikato University profile](https://apps.mngt.waikato.ac.nz/Newsroom/StudentProfile/3724)). She worked as a researcher for Phil Goff and Helen Clark, then in London as a policy adviser in the UK Cabinet Office, and in 2008 was elected president of the International Union of Socialist Youth. She was raised in the LDS Church but left it in 2005, citing her support for gay rights ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/lifestyle/news/article.cfm?c_id=6&objectid=11789352)). She married broadcaster Clarke Gayford in January 2024; their daughter Neve was born on 21 June 2018 while Ardern was prime minister ([BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-44568537)). ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 49th | 2008–2011 | List | 20 | Labour | | 50th | 2011–2014 | List | 13 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | List | 5 | Labour | | 51st | 2017 (by-election)– | Mount Albert | | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Mount Albert | 1 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Mount Albert | 1 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 40th Prime Minister of New Zealand | 26 October 2017 | 25 January 2023 | | | 17th Leader of the Labour Party | 1 August 2017 | 22 January 2023 | | | 36th Leader of the Opposition | 1 August 2017 | 26 October 2017 | | | 17th Deputy Leader of the Labour Party | 7 March 2017 | 1 August 2017 | | | Member of the New Zealand Parliament | 8 November 2008 | 15 April 2023 | | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - **List MP, 2008–2017.** Entered Parliament from list position 20 in 2008 (losing the Waikato electorate). Stood in Auckland Central in 2011 and 2014, losing to National's Nikki Kaye by 717 and then 600 votes ([2011 results](http://www.electionresults.org.nz/electionresults_2011/electorate-1.html), [2014 results](http://www.electionresults.org.nz/electionresults_2014/electorate-1.html)). Spokesperson for youth affairs (under Goff), social development (No. 4 in Shearer's shadow cabinet, 2011), then justice, children, small business and arts (under Little, 2014). - **Mount Albert, 2017–2023.** Won the February 2017 Mount Albert by-election with about 77% of the vote ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=11807614)); majorities of 15,264 (2017) and 21,246 (2020) ([2017](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/electorate-details-27.html), [2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-24.html)). - **Deputy leader (7 Mar 2017) and leader (1 Aug 2017).** Became leader seven weeks before the 2017 election after Andrew Little resigned; Labour rose from 24% to the low 40s in polls ("Jacindamania") and won 46 seats ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=11922098)). - **Prime Minister, 26 Oct 2017 – 25 Jan 2023.** Led a Labour–NZ First coalition with Green confidence and supply (2017–2020), then the first single-party majority government under MMP after winning 65 seats and 50% of the party vote in 2020 ([Electoral Commission](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/)). Also Minister for National Security and Intelligence, Arts, Culture and Heritage, and the first Minister for Child Poverty Reduction. - **Resignation.** Announced on 19 January 2023 that she no longer had "enough in the tank", resigned as leader on 22 January and as PM on 25 January, and left Parliament in April 2023 ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/jan/19/jacinda-ardern-resigns-as-prime-minister-of-new-zealand)). ## Record & notable actions - **Christchurch mosque attacks (2019):** led the national response to the 15 March 2019 attacks in which 51 people were killed; within a month Parliament banned most semi-automatic weapons and high-capacity magazines, followed by a buy-back ([NYT](https://www.nytimes.com/2019/04/10/world/asia/new-zealand-guns-jacinda-ardern.html)); co-founded the Christchurch Call with Emmanuel Macron ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12226274)). - **COVID-19:** border closure (March 2020), alert-level 4 lockdown, elimination strategy until October 2021, vaccine rollout from February 2021 ([NYT](https://www.nytimes.com/2021/10/04/world/australia/new-zealand-covid-zero.html)). The MIQ system left many citizens unable to return; in April 2022 the High Court found aspects of MIQ unjustifiably limited citizens' right to enter New Zealand ([High Court judgment](https://www.courtsofnz.govt.nz/assets/Uploads/Judgments-online/2022-NZHC-832.pdf)). - **Child poverty and welfare:** Child Poverty Reduction Act targets; the 2018 Families Package (26 weeks' paid parental leave, Best Start payment) ([Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/feature/supporting-new-zealand-families-0)); free school lunches (Ka Ora, Ka Ako); benefit increases; first year of tertiary study fees-free (2018). - **Climate:** Zero Carbon Act passed with cross-party support (2019); declared a climate emergency in December 2020 ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/dec/02/new-zealand-declares-a-climate-change-emergency)). - **Tax:** ruled out a capital gains tax under her leadership in April 2019 after the Tax Working Group recommended one ([RNZ](https://www.radionz.co.nz/news/on-the-inside/387347/week-in-politics-labour-s-biggest-campaign-burden-scrapped)); bright-line test extended to 10 years (2021). - **Other:** formal apology for the Dawn Raids (2021); cannabis referendum (2020, narrowly defeated; she disclosed afterwards she voted yes) ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/123261775/pm-defends-no-comment-stance-on-cannabis-referendum)). - **Conscience votes:** voted for marriage equality (2013) and for the Abortion Legislation Act 2020 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/412087/abortion-legislation-bill-passes-third-and-final-reading-in-parliament)). ## Controversies - **Clare Curran (2018):** criticised for initially only removing Curran from Cabinet over an undisclosed meeting rather than dismissing her; Curran later resigned ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2018/09/prime-minister-jacinda-ardern-accepts-clare-curran-s-resignation-as-a-minister.html)). - **Labour staffer sexual-assault complaint (2019):** her account that she had been told the complaint did not involve sexual assault was questioned by media; party president Nigel Haworth resigned ([The Spinoff timeline](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/11-09-2019/timeline-labour-staffer-misconduct-inquiry/)). - by 9,370 in 2023); a list MP since 2017 ([2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-52.html); [2023](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-52.html); Minister of Education and Child Poverty Reduction (No. 6 in Cabinet) from 31 January 2023 ([Beehive list](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2023-01/Ministerial%20List%20as%20announced%20on%2031%20January%202023.pdf)). - **Opposition:** education and women (2023–2025); workplace relations, social investment, ECE and child poverty (from March 2025). ## Controversies - **Privileges Committee referral (2023):** Speaker Adrian Rurawhe referred her to the Privileges Committee after she delayed correcting a February 2023 statement to the House that she had no role in the timing of school attendance data release; she was told of the error but did not correct it until 2 May. On 29 June 2023 the committee found she had not intentionally misled the House but had acted with a "high degree of negligence", and required her to apologise to the House. Hipkins kept her as minister ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/490981/education-minister-jan-tinetti-s-delay-in-correcting-record-to-be-investigated); [RNZ report](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/492852/jan-tinetti-made-error-of-judgement-that-misled-parliament-privileges-committee-finds)). After losing Tauranga in 2023 she said a "weight had been lifted", a remark criticised by breakfast-TV hosts ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2023/10/election-2023-am-hosts-slam-bizarre-reactions-from-ousted-labour-mps-jan-tinetti-dan-rosewarne.html)). ## 2026 candidacy - # Kelvin Davis | | | |---|---| | **Party** | Labour | | **Status (Oct 2026)** | Former MP | | **Born** | 1967-03-02 — Kawakawa, New Zealand | | **Electorate(s) held** | Te Tai Tokerau | | **Parliaments** | 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54 | | **First elected** | 2008 | | **Key roles** | 18th Deputy Leader of the Labour Party (2017–2023)
14th Minister of Corrections (2017–2023)
1st Minister for Māori–Crown Relations (2017–2023)
3rd Minister for Children (2020–2023)
36th Minister of Tourism (2017–2020)
Deputy Leader of the Opposition (2017) | | **Wikipedia** | [Kelvin Davis (politician)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin_Davis_%28politician%29) | ## Current status Davis left Parliament on Waitangi Day, 6 February 2024, having said during the campaign that he would not stay on as a list MP if he lost Te Tai Tokerau ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/301027449/kelvin-davis-calls-time-on-politics-career-will-end-at-waitangi)); Shanan Halbert replaced him. He indicated he would work as an Indigenous-relations consultant in Australia ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/504804/labour-mp-kelvin-davis-message-to-national-as-he-leaves-politics-back-to-the-bad-old-times)). In 2026 the National-led government appointed him to the Māori Education Ministerial Advisory Group for two years from May 2026 ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/former-labour-deputy-kelvin-davis-joins-erica-stanfords-maori-advisory-education-group/SQXBBGJK3VBKZCCFKHFBI2BIZU/)). He is not a 2026 candidate. ## Biography Born 2 March 1967 in Kawakawa and raised at Karetu in the Bay of Islands (Ngāpuhi, Ngāti Manu), Davis trained at Auckland College of Education and spent 20 years in education, including as principal of Karetu School (1994–1998) and Kaitaia Intermediate (2001–2007), which he was credited with turning around ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/99182567/national-portrait-kelvin-davis--minister-of-sunshine)). He is married to Moira; they have three children. ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 49th | 2008–2011 | List | 33 | Labour | | 50th | 2014– | List | 23 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | Te Tai Tokerau | 18 | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Te Tai Tokerau | 2 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Te Tai Tokerau | 2 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–2024 | List | 2 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 18th Deputy Leader of the Labour Party | 1 August 2017 | 7 November 2023 | | | 14th Minister of Corrections | 26 October 2017 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 1st Minister for Māori–Crown Relations | 26 October 2017 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 3rd Minister for Children | 6 November 2020 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 36th Minister of Tourism | 26 October 2017 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | | Deputy Leader of the Opposition | 1 August 2017 | 26 October 2017 | | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - **List MP 2008–2011;** lost Te Tai Tokerau to Hone Harawira in 2008, the 2011 by-election and the 2011 general election, and left Parliament. - **Returned May 2014** as a list MP when Shane Jones resigned, then won Te Tai Tokerau from Harawira in September 2014 — ending Internet-Mana's parliamentary presence — after endorsements from John Key and Winston Peters ([Stuff](http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/10524510/Davis-win-a-critical-blow-for-Harawira-Internet-Mana)). Held it in 2017 (majority 4,807 over Harawira) and 2020; lost it in 2023 to Te Pāti Māori's Mariameno Kapa-Kingi by 517 votes ([2017](http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/electorate-details-69.html), [2023](https://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-70.html)). - **Deputy Labour leader, 1 Aug 2017 – Nov 2023** under Ardern and Hipkins. Declined to be deputy prime minister in 2020; Grant Robertson took the role ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300147451/kelvin-davis-wont-seek-the-role-of-deputy-prime-minister-but-wants-to-stay-on-deputy-labour-leader)). - **Minister, 2017–2023:** No. 3 in Cabinet; first Minister for Māori–Crown Relations: Te Arawhiti, Minister of Corrections (2017–2023), Tourism (2017–2020), Children (2020–2023), Associate Education (Māori). Acting prime minister on several occasions. ## Record & notable actions - **Prison population:** as Corrections Minister he set out to reduce Māori imprisonment; the imprisonment rate fell from about 213 to 149 per 100,000 during his tenure, helped by bail support and earlier parole-readiness programmes — National's Mark Mitchell argued the focus should have been on reducing crime ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/election-2023-labour-dumps-prison-population-reduction-target/AAL2EXLUGBFNHJ27VJSRS2EPHY/); [The Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/02-11-2018/kelvin-davis-has-a-cunning-plan-to-cut-the-prison-population-and-its-working)). - **Te Arawhiti:** established the Office for Māori Crown Relations in 2018 ([Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/te-arawhiti-%E2%80%98bridge%E2%80%99-better-m%C4%81ori-crown-relations-launched-parliament)). - **Oranga Tamariki:** declined to back chief executive Grainne Moss (who resigned in January 2021), set up a ministerial advisory board, and began devolving services to iwi and community providers ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/435242/new-four-person-board-to-oversee-oranga-tamariki-overhaul)). - **In opposition (2014–2017):** exposed problems at Serco-run Mount Eden prison, after which Serco lost the contract ([Stuff](http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/70619419/labours-kelvin-davis-says-mt-eden-prison-guard-revelations-are-corruption)); his KiwiBuild member's bill (10,000 homes a year) was defeated in 2017. - **Conscience votes:** voted for the End of Life Choice Act 2019 and the Abortion Legislation Act 2020. Broke with Labour policy to support the two charter schools in his electorate, which became state-integrated ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/335647/davis-threatens-to-resign-if-two-charter-schools-closed-down)). ## Controversies - **Parliamentary performance:** his performances as acting PM in the House were widely criticised (one Stuff columnist called a 2017 appearance a "trainwreck") ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/opinion/98982731/labour-has-a-problem--we-need-to-talk-about-acting-prime-minister-kelvin-davis)). - **Waikeria Prison riot (2020–21):** criticised by National and Te Pāti Māori for staying silent during the six-day standoff; he pushed back on parts of the Chief Ombudsman's later report on Corrections ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/kahu/kelvin-davis-pushes-back-on-the-ombudsmans-damming-corrections-report/CYJFPMX3IFBJNEHR3STID6VNV4/)). - **"Vanilla lens" remark (2022):** told ACT's Karen Chhour (who is Ngāpuhi) to stop looking through a "vanilla lens"; ACT called it racist and he apologised to her by phone ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/475720/minister-davis-apologises-over-comments-to-act-s-karen-chhour)). ## 2026 candidacy Not listed as a Labour candidate for the 2026 election on policy.nz (Oct 2026). ## Sources - parties/labour/people/kerrin-leoni/READM: # Kerrin Leoni | | | |---|---| | **Party** | Labour | | **Status (Oct 2026)** | 2026 candidate (not previously an MP) | | **Born** | 1979 or 1980 | | **2026 candidacy** | Tāmaki Makaurau · list #43 | | **Key roles** | Auckland Councillor for the Whau ward (2022–2025) | | **Wikipedia** | [Kerrin Leoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerrin_Leoni) | ## Current status On 22 October 2026 Te Ao Māori News released video of Leoni wearing Labour campaign branding at a Mongrel Mob gathering in Papakura on 3 October, where she urged attendees to vote ([Te Ao Māori News](https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2026/10/22/video-shows-labour-candidate-kerrin-leoni-at-mongrel-mob-event/)). Chris Hipkins initially accepted her account. On 23 October Leoni resigned as a Labour candidate, and Hipkins said the footage was "inconsistent with the standards" expected of Labour candidates. Because nominations had closed, her name remains on the ballot but without Labour's endorsement ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/election-2026-live-updates-kerrin-leoni-resigns-as-labour-candidate-after-campaigning-with-mongrel-mob/R5IJCEB4TNF3LETYQ5JOSBPH7A/)). His member's bill allowing on-licence premises open on Good Friday, Anzac Day morning and Christmas Day to sell alcohol under normal conditions passed its third reading 66–55 on a conscience vote on 1 April 2026 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/591281/bill-to-ease-holiday-alcohol-restrictions-passes-final-reading-in-parliament)). ## Biography Born in Eketāhuna in 1985 and adopted into a long-established Wairarapa Labour family, McAnulty was head boy of Chanel College (2002) and gained a BA, PGDipArts and an MA in politics from the University of Otago ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/kieran-mcanulty-why-the-wairarapa-mp-is-rural-to-the-core/SVEH6NYJJZHJNFPGBO4CSZF7PU/)). He worked as a TAB bookmaker and an economic development adviser at Masterton District Council, and was a volunteer firefighter ([maiden statement](https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/hansard-debates/rhr/document/HansS_20171116_064200000/mcanulty-kieran)). He was treasurer of the New Zealand Republic campaign. In January 2024 he married Gia Garrick, a former press secretary to the prime minister. His battered red Mazda ute became a campaign trademark until he sold it for charity in 2021 ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2021/09/19/labours-mcanulty-swapping-famous-red-ute-for-hybrid-wagon/)). ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 52nd | 2017–2020 | List | 38 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Wairarapa | 26 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–present | List | 16 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 20th Minister of Local Government | 1 February 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 2nd Minister for Rural Communities | 1 February 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 28th Minister for Emergency Management | 14 June 2022 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 14th Minister for Racing | 14 June 2022 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | Chief Government Whip in the House of Representatives | 2 November 2020 | 14 June 2022 | Jacinda Ardern | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Opposition portfolios (as of 11 March 2026) Rank 7 in Chris Hipkins' shadow cabinet: - Shadow Leader of the House - Spokesperson for Housing - Spokesperson for Infrastructure - Spokesperson for Public Investment _Source: [Shadow Cabinet of Chris Hipkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Cabinet_of_Chris_Hipkins), list as of 11 March 2026._ ### Career summary - **Wairarapa:** lost to National's Alastair Scott in 2014 and 2017 (entering Parliament from list position 38 in 2017); won the seat in 2020 by 6,545 votes over Mike Butterick; lost it to Butterick in 2023 and returned on the list ([2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-58.html); [2023](https://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-58.html)). - **Whip:** junior whip (2017–2020), chief whip (2020–2022) ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/hawkes-bay-today/news/wairarapa-mp-elected-chief-government-whip/YNOLUT76J4HXT2JUW4H27U3X44/)). - **Minister, 2022–2023:** Minister for Emergency Management and Racing (outside Cabinet) from June 2022; in Cabinet from 31 January 2023 as Minister of Local Government, Rural Communities and Deputy Leader of the House; Regional Development from July 2023 ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/131110270/prime-minister-chris-hipkins-reveals-his-new-cabinet)). - **Opposition:** No. 7 in the shadow cabinet, with housing, local government and regional development (2023); Shadow Leader of the House; from March 2025 housing, infrastructure and public investment. ## Record & notable actions - **Cyclone Gabrielle:** declared a national state of emergency on 14 February 2023 — only the third in New Zealand's history ([Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/state-national-emergency-declared)). - **Three Waters reset (April 2023):** restructured the reform into ten regional water entities while keeping the council/mana whenua co-governance model ([Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/major-shakeup-will-see-affordable-water-reforms-led-and-delivered-regionally)); the reforms were repealed by the next government. - Led the Local Electoral (Advertising) Amendment Act 2022 through the House. - **Conscience votes:** supports marriage equality, voted for the Abortion Legislation Act 2020, and voted yes in both 2020 referendums (cannabis and euthanasia) ([Parliament Hansard](https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/hansard-debates/rhr/combined/HansDeb_20200318_20200318_24)). - **Member's bill:** his bill easing alcohol trading restrictions on Good Friday, Anzac Day and Christmas Day (excluding bottle stores and supermarkets) became law with royal assent on 2 April 2026 ([ODT](https://www.odt.co.nz/news/dunedin/mixed-response-alcohol-act-changes)). ## Controversies - **Gaurav Sharma allegations (2022):** expelled MP Gaurav Sharma accused McAnulty, then chief whip, of bullying; Labour and Ardern rejected the claims ([The Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/live-updates/12-08-2022)). - **Accommodation allowance (2024):** The Post reported he claimed a $36,400-a-year allowance to rent a Lower Hutt flat from his wife while owning a home in Masterton ([The Post](https://www.thepost.co.nz/politics/350305871/labours-kieran-mcanulty-claims-housing-perk-live-wifes-apartment)). - **Ejections from the House:** in 2019 (mocking Simon Bridges) and on 19 February 2026, after accusing Speaker Gerry Brownlee of "double standards" over Winston Peters' remarks about the name Aotearoa ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/labour-mp-kieran-mcanulty-booted-from-the-house-over-speakers-handling-of-winston-peters-racist-remark/MR2AVPBXJBHCJH7AFODN3MICJA/)). ## 2026 candidacy - # Kiri Allan | | | |---|---| | **Party** | Labour | | **Status (Oct 2026)** | Former MP | | **Born** | 1984 — Te Karaka, New Zealand | | **Electorate(s) held** | East Coast | | **Parliaments** | 52, 53 | | **First elected** | 2017 | | **Key roles** | 51st Minister of Justice (2022–2023)
Minister for Regional Development (2023)
14th Minister of Conservation (2020–2022)
27th Minister for Emergency Management (2020–2022) | | **Wikipedia** | [Kiri Allan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiri_Allan) | ## Current status Allan did not stand in 2023 and left Parliament at that election. After leaving she announced a book deal with Penguin and set up a lobbying consultancy — registered while she was still an MP, which drew "revolving door" criticism given she had been responsible for lobbying reform as justice minister ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/political-roundup-kiri-allan-latest-ex-labour-minister-to-move-into-lobbying/HBUTCMXLNRGQTGWLA2EFOGMGZY/)). She is not a 2026 candidate. ## Biography Kiritapu Allan was born in 1984 in Te Karaka (Ngāti Ranginui, Ngāti Tūwharetoa) and raised whāngai by an aunt and uncle in Paengaroa and later Auckland, where she attended Auckland Girls' Grammar's reo Māori unit ([E-Tangata](https://e-tangata.co.nz/korero/kiri-allan-always-raising-eyebrows/)). She left school at 16, worked at KFC and as a fruit picker, then studied law and politics at Victoria University of Wellington, interning for Helen Clark and lawyer Annette Sykes. She worked at ChenPalmer and Kāhui Legal in Whakatāne. She has written about undergoing conversion therapy as a teenager ([The Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/19-02-2022/kiri-allan-my-conversion-therapy-story)). She was treated for stage 3 cervical cancer in 2021 and declared cancer-free that December ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/457582/mp-kiri-allan-given-all-clear-after-months-of-cervical-cancer-treatment)). ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 52nd | 2017–2020 | List | 21 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | East Coast | 25 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 51st Minister of Justice | 14 June 2022 | 24 July 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | Minister for Regional Development | 1 February 2023 | 24 July 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 14th Minister of Conservation | 6 November 2020 | 14 June 2022 | Jacinda Ardern | | 27th Minister for Emergency Management | 6 November 2020 | 14 June 2022 | Jacinda Ardern | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - **List MP 2017–2020** after losing East Coast to Anne Tolley; junior whip, chair of Labour's rural caucus. - **East Coast MP 2020–2023:** won the open seat by 6,331 votes over National's Tania Tapsell ([2020 results](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-09.html)). - **Minister:** Conservation and Emergency Management (Nov 2020 – Jun 2022) plus associate Arts, Culture and Heritage and Environment; Justice and Associate Finance from June 2022; under Hipkins (No. 10 in Cabinet) also Regional Development and Associate Transport, and a lead minister for the Cyclone Gabrielle response in Tairāwhiti ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/483394/prime-minister-chris-hipkins-reveals-cabinet-reshuffle)). Co-nominated Hipkins for the leadership in January 2023. ## Record & notable actions - Fronted the March 2021 Kermadec earthquake tsunami evacuations on the day her cancer diagnosis was confirmed ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300269974/kiri-allan-bit-of-a-superwoman-to-handle-tsunami-and-earthquake-response-on-same-day-as-medical-test-confirming-her-cancer-diagnosis)). - Passed the law creating the Matariki public holiday (first observed 2022) ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/464833/matariki-public-holiday-passes-into-law)). - As Justice Minister: repealed the three-strikes sentencing law (2022) ([Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/three-strikes-legislation-repeal-bill-passes-third-reading)); electoral law reforms (donations disclosure, Māori electoral option); expanded legal aid; announced a new ram-raid offence in July 2023. - **Conscience votes:** voted for the third readings of the End of Life Choice Bill and Abortion Legislation Bill (having voted against the euthanasia bill at second reading). ## Controversies - **RNZ speech (March 2023):** at the farewell of her then-fiancée Māni Dunlop from RNZ, she commented on RNZ's treatment of Māori staff; she accepted this could be seen as a minister directing a Crown entity and apologised ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/489511/rnz-releases-comments-from-kiri-allan-speech)). - **Meng Foon donations (April 2023):** she had properly declared 2020 campaign support from Race Relations Commissioner Meng Foon, but was criticised for not flagging a conflict of interest when she became the minister responsible for him ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/04/21/allan-declares-perceived-conflict-of-interest-after-foon-donation/)). - **Staff treatment (June–July 2023):** the heads of DOC and NEMA raised concerns about how staff in her office were treated; she apologised and received coaching ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/493729/east-coast-mp-kiri-allan-to-resume-duties-after-speaking-with-pm-on-staff-allegations)). - **Arrest and resignation (July 2023):** on 23 July 2023 she crashed her ministerial car into a parked car in Wellington, was arrested for careless driving and refusing to accompany a police officer, and received an excess-breath-alcohol infringement notice; she resigned all portfolios the next day and announced she would not stand again ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/494338/kiri-allan-charged-with-reckless-driving-and-resisting-arrest-resigns-as-justice-minister-pm-says); [1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/07/25/kiri-allan-announces-she-wont-stand-for-re-election/)). In May 2024 she pleaded guilty to both charges; she was fined $300 and ordered to pay $5,296 reparation for careless driving and discharged on the second charge ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2024/05/22/kiri-allan-pleads-guilty-on-day-trial-was-set-to-begin/)). She has spoken publicly about her mental health at the time and later disclosed ADHD and PTSD diagnoses ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2024/01/26/kiri-allan-opens-up-about-days-that-led-to-her-political-downfall/)). ## 2026 candidacy Not listed as a Labour candidate for the 2026 election on policy.nz (Oct 2026). ## Sources - He is not a 2026 candidate. ## Biography Born 23 June 1976 to parents from Fakaofo, Tokelau, and raised in Christchurch, Faafoi trained at the New Zealand Broadcasting School and reported for TVNZ and the BBC before becoming Labour leader Phil Goff's chief press secretary in 2008 ([E-Tangata](https://e-tangata.co.nz/korero/kris-faafoi-a-minister-on-the-rise/)). He lives in Wellington with his wife Mae and three sons; his brother is broadcaster Jason Faafoi. ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 49th | 2010–2011 | Mana | | Labour | | 50th | 2011–2014 | Mana | 41 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | Mana | none | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Mana | 20 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2022 | List | 15 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 50th Minister of Justice | 6 November 2020 | 14 June 2022 | Jacinda Ardern | | 26th Minister for Broadcasting and Media | 7 September 2018 | 14 June 2022 | Jacinda Ardern | | 57th Minister of Immigration | 22 July 2020 | 14 June 2022 | Jacinda Ardern | | 13th Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs | 26 October 2017 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | | Minister for Government Digital Services | 27 June 2019 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | | 25th Minister of Civil Defence | 26 October 2017 | 27 June 2019 | Jacinda Ardern | | 64th Minister of Customs | 20 September 2018 | 27 June 2019 | Jacinda Ardern | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - **Minister 2017–2022:** Civil Defence and Commerce and Consumer Affairs (2017), Customs (2018), Broadcasting, Communications and Digital Media (from September 2018, after Clare Curran), Government Digital Services (2019), Immigration (from July 2020), and in Cabinet as Minister of Justice from November 2020 ([DPMC 2020](https://dpmc.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2020-11/ministerial-list-2-nov-2020.pdf)). - Announced on 13 June 2022 he would leave Parliament to spend more time with his family ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/128948673/kris-faafoi-trevor-mallard-to-quit-parliament-sparking-big-labour-reshuffle)). ## Record & notable actions - **Conversion practices ban:** introduced the Conversion Practices Prohibition Legislation Bill (July 2021), which passed its third reading on 15 February 2022 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/461599/politicians-react-as-bill-to-ban-conversion-therapy-passes)). -
