parties/labour/people/louisa-wall/README: # Louisa Wall | | | |---|---| | **Party** | Labour | | **Status (Oct 2026)** | Former MP | | **Born** | 1972-02-17 — Taupō, New Zealand | | **Electorate(s) held** | Manurewa | | **Parliaments** | 48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53 | | **First elected** | 2008 | | **Wikipedia** | [Louisa Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisa_Wall) | ## Current status Wall left Parliament on 1 May 2022, saying her departure was part of an agreement made during the disputed 2020 Manurewa selection and that it was "not entirely my choice" ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/465300/departing-labour-mp-louisa-wall-this-was-not-entirely-my-choice)). She was then Ambassador for Gender Equality (Pacific), a newly created role that critics said was designed for her; it was disestablished after two years ([Newsroom](http://newsroom.co.nz/2022/05/31/inside-louisa-walls-diplomatic-sinecure/); [The Post](https://www.thepost.co.nz/politics/350212701/louisa-walls-ambassador-role-scrapped)). In 2023 RNZ reported she was considering standing for Te Pāti Māori, which did not happen ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/488115/former-labour-mp-louisa-wall-could-stand-for-te-pati-maori-in-manurewa)). ## Biography Born 17 February 1972 in Taupō (Ngāti Tūwharetoa, Ngāti Hineuru, Waikato), Wall is a double international: a Silver Fern (netball, 1989–1992) and a Black Fern (rugby, 1995–2001) who won the 1998 Women's Rugby World Cup ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11893700)). She holds social work and social policy degrees from Massey and worked in health research for the Health Research Council, the Children's Commissioner and Counties Manukau DHB. She married lawyer Prue Kapua in 2015. ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 48th | 2008– | List | 46 | Labour | | 49th | 2011– | List | 43 | Labour | | 50th | 2011–2014 | Manurewa | none | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | Manurewa | 12 | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Manurewa | 26 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2022 | List | 27 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Career summary - List MP Feb–Nov 2008 and Apr–Nov 2011; **Manurewa MP 2011–2020** (majority 8,610 in 2011) — the first Māori Labour candidate to win a general electorate; list MP 2020–2022 after withdrawing from a disputed Manurewa selection won by Arena Williams ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12335909)). - Chaired the Health Committee (2017–2020); never a minister. Stuff's Henry Cooke judged she achieved more than any other Labour MP in opposition (2008–2017) ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300553289/louisa-wall-achieved-a-lot-in-politics-but-sometimes-forgot-it-was-a-team-sport)). ## Record & notable actions - **Marriage equality:** her Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill passed 77–44 on 17 April 2013, making New Zealand the 13th country to legalise same-sex marriage ([TVNZ](http://tvnz.co.nz/national-news/mps-vote-legalise-same-sex-marriage-5409720)). - **Abortion safe areas:** her bill restoring safe zones around abortion services passed 108–12 on 16 March 2022 ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/128080358/safe-areas-abortion-law-passes-with-large-majority-in-parliament)). - **Revenge porn:** her Harmful Digital Communications amendment passed unanimously on 2 March 2022. - Supported the End of Life Choice Act at every stage; an outspoken critic of China's treatment of Uyghurs (Ardern said she spoke as IPAC co-chair, not for the government) ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2021/07/jacinda-ardern-distances-herself-from-labour-mp-louisa-wall-who-accused-china-of-harvesting-organs.html)). ## Controversies - **2020 Manurewa selection and exit:** she called her de-selection unconstitutional and alleged Ardern did not want her in caucus because she had backed David Cunliffe; Ardern did not attend her valedictory speech ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300563234/pm-jacinda-ardern-will-not-attend-louisa-walls-valedictory-speech)). - **Al Nisbet cartoons:** her complaint over 2013 cartoons about Māori and Pacific families was dismissed by the Human Rights Review Tribunal and on appeal, though the High Court called the cartoons objectively offensive ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/labour-mps-racist-cartoon-appeal-against-fairfax-media-dismissed/K4QZ7ZJHBFEK5G3COO2DOTA4E4/)). ## 2026 candidacy Not listed as a Labour candidate for the 2026 election on policy.nz (Oct 2026). ## Sources - # Nanaia Mahuta | | | |---|---| | **Party** | Labour | | **Status (Oct 2026)** | Former MP | | **Born** | 1970-08-21 — Auckland, New Zealand | | **Electorate(s) held** | Te Tai Hauāuru, Tainui, Hauraki-Waikato | | **Parliaments** | 45, 46, 47, 48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53 | | **First elected** | 1996 | | **Key roles** | 28th Minister of Foreign Affairs (2020–2023)

12th Minister of Local Government (2017–2023)
44th Minister for Māori Development (2017–2020) | | **Wikipedia** | [Nanaia Mahuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanaia_Mahuta) | ## Current status Mahuta left Parliament after losing Hauraki-Waikato by 2,911 votes in 2023; she had not sought a list place ([2023 results](https://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-66.html)). She resigned her ministerial warrants on 11 November 2023 during the caretaker period. In 2025 she was one of ten current and former women MPs on the "People's Select Committee" convened by former National MP Marilyn Waring to hear submissions on the government's pay-equity changes ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/562148/pay-equity-changes-people-s-select-committee-formed-to-gather-evidence-instead-of-high-flying-cliches)). She is not a 2026 candidate. ## Biography Born 21 August 1970 in Auckland, Mahuta is the daughter of Sir Robert Mahuta (adopted son of Māori King Korokī) and a first cousin of the late Kiingi Tūheitia ([E-Tangata](https://e-tangata.co.nz/korero/no-silver-spoon/)). She was educated at Rakaumanga kura in Huntly and Waikato Diocesan School, and holds an MA (Hons) in social anthropology from the University of Auckland. She is married to Gannin Ormsby. In 2016 she became the first woman MP to wear a moko kauae ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2016/aug/11/first-woman-mp-maori-facial-tattoo-nz-parliament-moko-kauae)); she was named one of the BBC's 100 Women in 2018. ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 45th | 1996–1999 | List | 8 | Labour | | 46th | 1999–2002 | Te Tai Hauāuru | 10 | Labour | | 47th | 2002–2005 | Tainui | 19 | Labour | | 48th | 2005–2008 | Tainui | none | Labour | | 49th | 2008–2011 | Hauraki-Waikato | 10 | Labour | | 50th | 2011–2014 | Hauraki-Waikato | 12 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | Hauraki-Waikato | 6 | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Hauraki-Waikato | none | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Hauraki-Waikato | 10 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 28th Minister of Foreign Affairs | 6 November 2020 | 11 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 11th Minister of Disarmament and Arms Control | 1 February 2023 | 11 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 12th Minister of Local Government | 26 October 2017 | 1 February 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 44th Minister for Māori Development | 26 October 2017 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - **MP 1996–2023:** elected on the list in 1996 aged 26 (then the youngest MP); MP for Te Tai Hauāuru (1999–2002), Tainui (2002–2008) and Hauraki-Waikato (2008–2023). Became Mother of the House in October 2022 ([Parliament](https://www.parliament.nz/en/visit-and-learn/mps-and-parliaments-1854-onwards/members-of-parliament-longest-shortest-oldest-youngest/)). - **Fifth Labour Government:** Minister of Customs and Youth Affairs (2005), Local Government (2007–2008). - **Opposition 2008–2017:** spokesperson for Māori affairs, education, energy and conservation; stood for leader in 2014, finishing fourth. - **Sixth Labour Government:** Minister of Local Government (2017–2023) and Māori Development (2017–2020); **Minister of Foreign Affairs, 6 Nov 2020 – Nov 2023** — the first woman and first Māori woman in the role ([Stuff](https://stuff.co.nz/national/politics/123271205/nanaia-mahuta-will-be-foreign-minister-and-the-first-woman-to-do-the-job)); Disarmament and Arms Control (2023). ## Record & notable actions - **Three Waters:** led the reform to move council water services into four large entities with council/mana whenua co-governance; the Water Services Entities Act passed on 7 December 2022 with only Labour's votes. She later acknowledged underestimating public opposition and problems with the advertising campaign ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2022/03/13/mahuta-admits-getting-things-wrong-with-three-waters-reform/); [Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/130704446/labour-alone-in-support-of-three-waters-bill-as-it-passes-into-law)). The reforms were restructured under Hipkins in 2023 and repealed by the National-led government's Water Services Acts Repeal Act 2024 ([Wikipedia: Three Waters reform programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Waters_reform_programme)). - **Māori wards:** passed the Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021, removing the ability of local polls to overturn council decisions to create Māori wards ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/437105/maori-wards-amendment-bill-passes-final-reading-in-parliament)). - **Foreign policy:** introduced the Russia Sanctions Act 2022 (passed unanimously on 9 March 2022); suspended high-level contact with Myanmar after the 2021 coup; joined Five Eyes statements on Hong Kong while saying New Zealand would not let Five Eyes dictate its China relationship (April 2021) ([Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/4/19/new-zealand-says-it-will-set-china-policy-not-us-led-five-eyes)). - Commissioned the Future for Local Government review (2021–2023) and appointed commissioners to run Tauranga City Council (2020), later extended to 2024. - **Conscience votes:** voted against the Abortion Legislation Act 2020 (but for safe-areas legislation in 2022); in 2004 voted against her party's foreshore and seabed bill at first and second reading, then for it at third reading. ## Controversies - **Tauranga commissioners:** legal reviews commissioned by critics argued her decisions to install and then extend commissioners may have been unlawful; Local Government NZ's president called the extension "disgusting" ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/463183/tauranga-city-commissioners-retained-until-july-2024-minister-says)). - **Family contracts (2022):** National questioned government contracts awarded to her husband's company and relatives; a Public Service Commission review found agencies had not properly managed conflicts but found "no evidence of favouritism, bias, or undue influence" ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/business/public-service-commission-finds-govt-agencies-were-substandard-in-their-processes-signing-contracts-with-companies-of-family-members-of-nanaia-mahuta/XAUV7FJUXJEWRGL72BRKC5NNJE/)). - **Entrenchment clause (Dec 2022):** supported a Green amendment entrenching water-asset ownership against Cabinet's position; Christopher Luxon called for her sacking, while Ardern defended her ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/480290/christopher-luxon-calls-for-nanaia-mahuta-to-be-sacked-over-entrenchment-clause)). - **7 October 2023 statement:** her initial statement on the Hamas attack, which called for a halt to violence without condemning Hamas, was criticised; she later said she had rejected MFAT advice to use stronger language ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/11/19/nanaia-mahuta-on-israel-gaza-tweet-cant-dwell-on-mistakes/)). - ACT criticised her limited overseas travel as foreign minister (2022) ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/australias-foreign-minister-penny-wong-putting-nanaia-mahuta-to-shame-with-solomons-trip-act/M4UFDB5MY2ICPY7BDR7WFSIUQQ/)). ## 2026 candidacy Not listed as a Labour candidate for the 2026 election on policy.nz (Oct 2026). ## Sources - On 6 March 2025 Winston Peters dismissed him after he questioned, at a Chatham House event, whether Donald Trump understood history (invoking Churchill's criticism of the Munich Agreement); Luxon backed the decision, Hipkins said Goff had "overstepped the mark", and Helen Clark accused the government of placating the Trump administration ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/mar/06/phil-goff-donald-trump-comments-new-zealand-high-commissioner-removed-chatham-house-ntwnfb); [Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360604666/comment-cost-phil-goff-his-job-high-commissioner)). He later said he had "no regrets" ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2025/04/04/no-regrets-phil-goff-breaks-silence-on-trump-remark-sacking/)). ## Biography Born 22 June 1953 and raised in Three Kings, Auckland, Goff left home at 16 to attend university, working at a freezing works and as a cleaner to gain an MA (first-class honours) in political studies at the University of Auckland; he later organised for the Insurance Workers Union ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/general/candidate-profile-phil-goff-2011100311)). Defence, Trade, Disarmament and Pacific Island Affairs, and Associate Finance (2005–2008). - **Labour leader and Leader of the Opposition, 11 Nov 2008 – 13 Dec 2011**; Labour fell to 27.5% in 2011 and he stood down. Later spokesperson for foreign affairs, then defence and Auckland. - Resigned from Parliament on 12 October 2016 after winning the Auckland mayoralty, triggering the Mt Roskill by-election won by Michael Wood ([NZ Gazette](https://www.gazette.govt.nz/notice/id/2016-ps5847)). ## Record & notable actions - Signed the New Zealand–China Free Trade Agreement in Beijing on 7 April 2008 ([Stuff](http://www.stuff.co.nz/4466946a27013.html)); involved in the 2001 decision to accept 131 Tampa refugees. - Introduced student fees and loans as tertiary education minister (late 1980s). - As opposition leader campaigned against raising GST to 15% and against mining on conservation land (2010). - As Auckland mayor (2016–2022) barred far-right speakers Lauren Southern and Stefan Molyneux from council venues (2018), prompting a free-speech legal challenge that was withdrawn ([RNZ](https://www.radionz.co.nz/news/national/362611/free-speech-coalition-withdraws-urgent-legal-action-over-goff-s-southern-molyneux-decision)), and opposed the Three Waters mandate (2021). ## Controversies - **SFO inquiry (2020–2022):** the Serious Fraud Office investigated his 2016 mayoral campaign's declaration of auction donations; After he said National MP Katie Nimon had been "lazy" for taking parental leave, Christopher Luxon said Nash would not be a minister in any government he led, and NZ First accepted Nash's resignation as a candidate on 22 July 2026; he later apologised to Nimon ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/772673/significant-distraction-stuart-nash-resigns-as-nz-first-candidate-after-sexist-comments)). In September 2025 he had resigned from his job at recruiter Robert Walters and from the Taxpayers' Union board after a crude on-air definition of a woman on The Platform ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/572769/former-labour-mp-stuart-nash-resigns-after-comment-about-women)). ## Biography Born in August 1967 and adopted by Jenny and Hal Nash — making him the adoptive great-grandson of Prime Minister Sir Walter Nash — he grew up in Napier, attended Napier Boys' High School, and gained master's degrees in law, forestry science and management from the University of Canterbury before working at AUT ([Parliament profile](https://www3.parliament.nz/en/mps-and-electorates/former-members-of-parliament/nash-stuart/)). He is married to Sarah Nash and has four children. ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 49th | 2008–2011 | List | 36 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | Napier | none | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Napier | 11 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Napier | 12 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 9th Minister for Economic Development | 1 February 2023 | 28 March 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 32nd Minister of Forestry | 6 November 2020 | 28 March 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 37th Minister of Tourism | 6 November 2020 | 1 February 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 11th Minister of Fisheries | 26 October 2017 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | | 30th Minister of Revenue | 26 October 2017 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - Contested Epsom for Labour in 2005; **list MP 2008–2011**; lost Napier to Chris Tremain in 2011 and briefly served as chief of staff to Labour leader David Shearer. - **Napier MP 2014–2023:** won with a 3,850 majority in 2014 (aided by Conservative Garth McVicar splitting the right vote), increased it in 2017, and held it by 5,856 in 2020 ([2014](http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2014/electorate-29.html); [2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-26.html)). - **Minister 2017–2023:** Police, Revenue, Small Business and Fisheries (2017–2020); Economic and Regional Development, Forestry, Tourism and Small Business (2020–2023); Police again (2023) until his resignation from that portfolio in March 2023 ([DPMC 2020](https://dpmc.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2020-11/ministerial-list-2-nov-2020.pdf)). ## Controversies - **Police independence (March 2023):** resigned as Police Minister after disclosing he had phoned the Police Commissioner urging an appeal of a sentence he considered too light ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/486012/stuart-nash-has-resigned-as-police-minister-pm-hipkins-says)). It then emerged the Attorney-General had reprimanded him in 2020 for comments about a murder accused before trial, and that he had lobbied MBIE for a constituent; Hipkins demoted him to the bottom of Cabinet on a "final warning" ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/486178/stuart-nash-demoted-to-bottom-of-cabinet-now-on-his-final-warning-hipkins)). - **Dismissal (28 March 2023):** sacked from all portfolios after it was revealed he had emailed two donors in 2020 about confidential Cabinet discussions on commercial rent relief ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/131627166/stuart-nash-sacked-as-minister-after-email-to-donors-emerged)). A Cabinet Office review in June 2023 found no further confidentiality breaches but identified an unmanaged conflict of interest over the appointment of donor Phil McCaw; the Chief Ombudsman found he had breached the Official Information Act by withholding the donor emails ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/492084/stuart-nash-did-not-share-confidential-information-with-other-donors-probe-finds); [Newsroom](https://www.newsroom.co.nz/stuart-nash-breached-official-information-laws-ombudsman)). after a private prosecution he pleaded guilty to fighting in a public place ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10483189)). - **Don Brash interjection (2006)** and crude 2002 remarks about rugby officials, for which he apologised. - **Defamation (2012):** sued with Andrew Little by Judith Collins over ACC comments; settled. - **False rape claim (2019–2021):** said in 2019 that a "rapist" worked at Parliament; the staffer sued, and Mallard apologised in December 2020, with the settlement and legal costs totalling about $333,000 of public money. National's motion of no confidence failed in February 2021; in May 2021 he repeated a sexual-assault allegation under privilege, which Ardern called "totally inappropriate" ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/trevor-mallard-defamation-case-settling-speakers-false-rape-claim-against-staffer-costs-taxpayers-333000-national/P2J7YX4WTQM3EZWLBCPAWPZGFM/)). - **Ambassadorship:** ACT criticised his appointment to Ireland as rewarding "bad behaviour" ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2022/10/trevor-mallard-s-salary-perks-in-ambassador-to-ireland-role-revealed.html)). ## 2026 candidacy Not listed as a Labour candidate for the 2026 election on policy.nz (Oct 2026). ## Sources - 3rd Leader of Mana Motuhake (2001–2003) | | **Wikipedia** | [Willie Jackson (politician)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Jackson_%28politician%29) | ## Current status Jackson is No. 4 on Labour's 2026 list (list-only) ([policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party)) and, since the 11 March 2026 reshuffle, Labour's spokesperson for Māori development, Māori–Crown relations and associate health (Māori) ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360949687/hipkins-reshuffles-labour-portfolios-henare-departs-and-plan-hatched-maori-seats-race)). He has again led Labour's campaign for the Māori electorates; Labour won only one of the seven in 2023, after which he said he had considered quitting ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/kahu/senior-mp-willie-jackson-to-leave-politics-following-hefty-defeat-at-the-polls-but-only-if-hes-not-wanted/MTUJK4PQDJBKFNX7PZNZOCAPLY/)). ## Biography Born in 1961 (Ngāti Maniapoto, Ngāti Porou), the son of urban Māori leaders Dame June Jackson and Bob Jackson; his uncles included activist Syd Jackson and lawyer Moana Jackson ([The Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/atea/28-02-2019/the-incredible-legacy-of-dame-june-jackson)). After leaving Māngere College he became a freezing worker and, at 21, president of the freezing workers' union. In the 1990s he ran Tangata Records and managed Moana and the Moahunters. A broadcaster for two decades, he ran Radio Waatea and Urban Māori Broadcasting, hosted *Eye to Eye* (TV One, 2004–2009) and talkback on RadioLive with John Tamihere. He chaired the National Urban Māori Authority (from 2003) and led the Manukau Urban Māori Authority (from 2009), whose subsidiary won a charter-school contract in 2017 ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/kahu/labour-candidate-willie-jackson-benefits-from-new-round-of-charter-schools/G676BTHOOKBLSAFRVUKYOFEZKE/)). ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 46th | 1999–2002 | List | 9 | Alliance (New Zealand political party) | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | List | 22 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | List | 19 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–present | List | 9 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 27th Minister of Broadcasting and Media | 14 June 2022 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 45th Minister for Māori Development | 6 November 2020 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 17th Minister of Employment | 26 October 2017 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | | 3rd Leader of Mana Motuhake | 2 June 2001 | 4 December 2003 | | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Opposition portfolios (as of 11 March 2026) Rank 5 in Chris Hipkins' shadow cabinet: - Spokesperson for Māori Development - Spokesperson for Māori Crown Relations - Associate Spokesperson for Health (Māori) _Source: [Shadow Cabinet of Chris Hipkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Cabinet_of_Chris_Hipkins), list as of 11 March 2026._ ### Career summary - **Alliance MP, 1999–2002** (Mana Motuhake); led Mana Motuhake from 2001 and was Alliance deputy leader at the 2002 election, when the party lost all its seats. - **Labour list MP, 2017–present.** Recruited by Andrew Little to run Labour's Māori-seat campaign in 2017, when Labour won all seven Māori electorates ([RNZ](http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/political/323829/willie-jackson-to-stand-for-labour)). - **Minister:** Minister of Employment (outside Cabinet) and Associate Minister for Māori Development, 2017–2020; Minister for Māori Development in Cabinet from November 2020, plus associate ACC and justice; Minister of Broadcasting and Media from June 2022 ([DPMC 2020](https://dpmc.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2020-11/ministerial-list-2-nov-2020.pdf)); co-chair of Labour's Māori caucus. - **Opposition:** Māori development, broadcasting, employment and associate portfolios (2023); Māori development and social development (March 2025); Māori development, Māori–Crown relations and associate health (Māori) (March 2026). ## Record & notable actions - **Public media merger:** introduced the Aotearoa New Zealand Public Media Bill to merge RNZ and TVNZ (2022); it was scrapped by the Hipkins government in February 2023 ([Parliament](https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/bills-and-laws/bills-proposed-laws/document/BILL_125298/aotearoa-new-zealand-public-media-bill); [Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/131174007/rnztvnz-merger-gone-minimum-wage-rises-policies-delayed-in-government-refocus)). - Apologised to Moriori on behalf of Ngāti Tama and Ngāti Mutunga as the Moriori Claims Settlement passed in 2021 ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/moriori-praised-for-dedication-patience-as-18m-and-apology-settlement-with-crown-becomes-law/VR32NHE6MDBEHZE6ZL5Z2X5NDU/)). - A leading opponent of ACT's Treaty Principles Bill; won a 2024 Oxford Union debate calling for the return of mokomōkai from the British Museum ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2024/05/24/willie-jackson-calls-for-return-of-mokomokai-in-oxford-debate-win/)). ## Controversies - **Roast Busters interview (2013):** he and John Tamihere were taken off air at RadioLive after an interview with a friend of an alleged victim in which the group's actions were described as "mischief" ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/roast-busters-radiolive-hosts-taken-off-air/C4HJSTJI55U546Q2OUS4OA7WUY/?c_id=1&objectid=11155132)). - **Jack Tame interview (Dec 2022):** a combative Q+A interview on the media merger, in which he questioned the host's motives, drew criticism including from Ardern; he gave a partial apology ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/480223/willie-jackson-gives-partial-apology-over-public-media-merger-interview)). - **"Go to war" remark (Nov 2023):** said Māori would "go to war" if the incoming government pursued a Treaty principles referendum; ACT leader David Seymour responded that people who "threaten war" instead of debate "are not being a good actor" ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2023/11/labour-mp-willie-jackson-warns-of-m-ori-uprising-over-act-s-proposed-treaty-referendum.html)). - **Ejections from the House:** in December 2021 (refusing to withdraw calling ACT "right-wing fascists"), November 2024 (calling David Seymour a liar during the Treaty Principles Bill first reading) and May 2025 ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/maori-development-minister-willie-jackson-kicked-out-of-parliament-for-right-wing-fascist-comment/OIZQJ3QM42VSM3GSSLE7YLLIYY/); [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/533792/watch-labour-s-willie-jackson-ejected-from-house-for-calling-david-seymour-a-liar-during-treaty-principles-bill-reading); [1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2025/05/15/labours-willie-jackson-booted-from-house/)). ## 2026 candidacy - Led the Mana Movement until May 2021. Not a 2026 candidate. ## Biography Born in Whangārei on 6 January 1955 to John and Titewhai Harawira (a prominent activist); of Ngāti Hau, Ngāti Wai, Ngāti Hine, Te Aupōuri, Ngāpuhi and Ngāti Whātua descent. Raised in West Auckland; attended St Stephen's School and the University of Auckland. A long-time activist — He Taua (1979), the 1981 Springbok tour protests, land occupations, Māori language and broadcasting, and the 2004 foreshore and seabed hīkoi. Married to Hilda Halkyard-Harawira. ## Political career - Won **Te Tai Tokerau** for the Māori Party in 2005 and 2008. - Clashed with the party over its support for the National-led government and the foreshore and seabed replacement law; suspended from caucus and left the party in February 2011. - Founded the **Mana Party** (April 2011), resigned to force a by-election and won it (June 2011, majority 1,117); re-elected in November 2011. - In 2014 Mana ran jointly with Kim Dotcom's Internet Party; Harawira lost to Labour's Kelvin Davis after National and NZ First urged tactical votes for Davis. Lost again to Davis in 2017. ## Record & notable actions - **"Feed the Kids" Bill** (Education (Breakfast and Lunch Programmes in Schools) Amendment Bill, drawn 2012): free meals in decile 1–2 schools — a forerunner of later school-lunch policy. - Arrested in 2012 at a Glen Innes state-house demolition protest; organised free breakfasts in South Auckland. - Led iwi COVID-19 checkpoints into the Far North in 2020–21 (some shut down by police). ## Controversies - A long record of inflammatory remarks: a 2009 profane email to Buddy Mikaere about "white motherf***ers" after skipping a European conference for Paris (he apologised for the wording, not the sentiment); calling John Howard a "racist bastard"; describing National's Māori MPs as John Key's "little house niggers" (2012); praising Osama bin Laden as a man who "fought for... his people" (2011, later apologised for how he expressed it); and in 2017 calling for the death penalty for Chinese methamphetamine importers. - Said in 2010 he "wouldn't feel comfortable" if his children brought home a Pākehā partner. ## Sources - https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hone_Harawira&oldid=1363715231 - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_P%C4%81ti_M%C4%81ori

## Current status

Former MP. He resigned on 21 July 2020 (see Controversies). His activities since are not detailed in the sources consulted.

## Biography

- **Early life:** born on 29 August 1983 in Ashburton. He boarded at Christchurch Boys' High School and studied political science and economics at the University of Canterbury.
- **Early politics:** stood list-only for ACT in 2005 and 2008.
- **Parliamentary staff:** from 2007, a parliamentary researcher, then a staffer in the offices of Rodney Hide, Phil Heatley and Steven Joyce.

## Political career

- **Rangitata (2017):** won the seat for National, beating Labour's Jo Luxton by 6,331 votes.
- **Spokesperson:** South Island regional development under Simon Bridges, then biosecurity under Todd Muller and Judith Collins.

**Roles held:**

- MP for Rangitata (2017–2020)
- National spokesperson for biosecurity; South Island regional development

## Record & notable actions

- **Conscience votes:** a social liberal; voted for the End of Life Choice and abortion bills.

**Conscience votes** (recorded third-reading votes):

## Controversies

- **Resignation (July 2020):**
  - On 20 July 2020 he announced he would not seek re-election, citing personal reasons.
  - It was then reported that he had sent a pornographic image to a 19-year-old student. He claimed someone else had used his phone.
  - Judith Collins said she "no longer trusted his story" after reports of further explicit messages to other women, and he resigned effective immediately on 21 July.
  - At least five women reported similar behaviour. Police investigated but did not lay charges.

# Cam Calder

| | |
|---|---|
| **Party** | New Zealand National Party |
| **Status** | Former MP |
| **Now (Oct 2026)** | Retired from Parliament at the 2014 election. Has since acted as a Commonwealth election observer (Sri Lanka, 2015) and written opinion pieces (NZ Herald, 2021). |
| **Electorate(s)** | List MP (2009–2014); contested Manurewa 2008, 2011 |

| **First elected** | 2009 (list vacancy) |

## Current status

Former MP. He retired at the 2014 election, and Simeon Brown replaced him as National's Manurewa candidate. He was a Commonwealth election observer in Sri Lanka in 2015. In 2021 he wrote a NZ Herald op-ed criticising the new NZ history curriculum.

## Biography

- **Early life:** born in 1952 and raised in New Plymouth.
- **Medicine:** trained as a dentist at Otago, then retrained in medicine at Cambridge. He worked as an emergency doctor in England and New Zealand, and later as clinical research director for an equipment company.
- **Other interests:** president of the French New Zealand Business Council and a pétanque promoter; he represented New Zealand at the 1995 world championships.
- **Personal:** married to Jenny; two children.

## Political career

- **Joined National:** 2003.
- **2008:** contested Manurewa (#58 on the list) and missed out when the final count cut National's seats by one.
- **List MP (June 2009):** entered Parliament when Richard Worth resigned, and was re-elected on the list in 2011.
- **Committees:** chaired the Education and Science Committee (2013–14); deputy chair of the Justice and Electoral Committee.

**Roles held:**

- List MP (2009–2014)
- Chair, Education and Science Committee (2013–2014)

## Record & notable actions

- **Laser pointers:** his member's bill restricting high-powered laser pointers in public places became law in July 2014.
- **Conscience votes:** voted for marriage equality (2013) and supported raising the alcohol purchase age to 20.

**Conscience votes** (recorded third-reading votes):

| Bill | Vote |
|---|---|
| [Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill — third reading, 17 Apr 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_(Definition_of_Marriage)_Amendment_Act_2013) | for |

## Controversies

None significant identified in the sources consulted.

| | |

## Current status

Former MP. He retired at the 2014 election, and Maureen Pugh replaced him as National's West Coast-Tasman candidate. According to Wikipedia he and his wife farm Highland cattle near Lake Brunner.

## Biography

- **Early life:** born on 7 March 1945 in Prestwick, Scotland. He attended Sandhurst.
- **New Zealand:** naturalised in 1980. He worked in exporting on the West Coast.
- **Other roles:** Uniting Church lay preacher and wedding celebrant.

## Political career

- **List MP (2005):** entered Parliament on the list after losing West Coast-Tasman.
- **West Coast-Tasman (2008):** won the seat from Labour's Damien O'Connor.
- **2011:** lost the seat back to O'Connor but was returned on the list.
- **Retirement:** announced in October 2013.

**Roles held:**

- MP for West Coast-Tasman (2008–2011)
- List MP (2005–2008, 2011–2014)

## Record & notable actions

- **Marriage equality:** a strong supporter of the 2013 bill; his second-reading speech was widely praised.
- **Celebrant:** officiated at Tau Henare's wedding in Parliament (2012).

**Conscience votes** (recorded third-reading votes):

None significant identified in the sources consulted.

He sat on the board of Virgin Australia from 2014 to 2016, while Air NZ held a stake. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/456886/christopher-luxon-set-to-be-new-national-party-leader-as-simon-bridges-withdraws)) - **2023 election:** National won 38.1% of the party vote and 48 seats, and Luxon held Botany with about 67%. ([DPMC](https://www.dpmc.govt.nz/publications/co-24-2-national-act-and-new-zealand-first-coalition-government-consultation-and-operating-arrangements)) - **Cabinet reshuffles:** - April 2024: Melissa Lee was removed from Cabinet, and Penny Simmonds lost the Disability Issues portfolio. - 19 January 2025: Simeon Brown took Health from Shane Reti, and Chris Bishop took Transport. - 2 April 2026: Penk entered Cabinet in Defence, Simmonds returned to Cabinet, and Bishop became Attorney-General but lost Leader of the House and campaign chair to Louise Upston and Simeon Brown. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/515100/media-minister-melissa-lee-demoted-from-cabinet-penny-simmonds-stripped-of-portfolio), [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/539370/as-it-happened-luxon-announces-cabinet-reshuffle-shane-reti-loses-health-portfolio-to-simeon-brown), [Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/pm-refreshes-ministerial-team)) **Roles held:** - Prime Minister of New Zealand (2023–) - Minister for National Security and Intelligence (2023–) - Minister Responsible for Ministerial Services (2023–) - Leader of the National Party (2021–) - Leader of the Opposition (2021–2023) - MP for Botany (2020–) - National spokesperson for local government, research, science, manufacturing and land information (2020–2021) ## Record & notable actions As Prime Minister, the government he leads has done the following (see [`../../track-record.md`](../../track-record.md) for the party-level record): - **Economy and spending:** - Delivered the NZ$14.7b tax relief package in Budget 2024. - Made public-service savings. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/562350/how-many-public-sector-jobs-have-really-been-axed)) - The economy was in recession through 2024. Unemployment rose from 3.7% (June 2023) to about 5.2% (late 2025). - **Law and order:** - Reinstated "three strikes" sentencing. - Banned gang patches in public. - Piloted a military-style academy (boot camp) for serious young offenders. - Ended funding for section 27 cultural reports. - **Treaty and Māori policy:** - Supported ACT's Treaty Principles Bill to first reading only, as the coalition agreement required. He later called Israel's conduct in Gaza "utterly, utterly appalling" (August 2025). - **Personal positions:** - He has said he is personally "pro-life", but that National would not change the Abortion Legislation Act 2020. - He voted for the Conversion Practices Prohibition Legislation Bill (2022) and gave National MPs a conscience vote on it. - He describes himself as a "soft republican". - He was not in Parliament for the 2013, 2019 and 2020 conscience votes. ## Controversies - **Accommodation allowance (2023–24):** he claimed about NZ$52,000 a year in accommodation support while living in his own Wellington apartment. ## Current status

Former MP and broadcaster. According to Wikipedia she reports for Radio Waatea from the Parliamentary Press Gallery, and she judged for the NZ International Film Festival in 2022.

## Biography

- **Early life:** born on 8 May 1961 in Auckland and raised in Mount Roskill. She is of Ngāti Porou, Te Whānau-ā-Apanui, Ngāpuhi, Ngāti Kuta and Ngāti Ruanui descent.
- **Education:** BA from Canberra College of Advanced Education.
- **Broadcasting:**
  - Founded the production company Front of the Box in 1993.
  - Executive producer and presenter of *Eye to Eye with Willie Jackson* (2004–09).
  - Produced the award-winning documentary *Children of the Revolution* (2008).
- **Personal:** civil union with Nadine Mau (2007); three children.

## Political career

- **2010:** stood for the Albert-Eden Local Board for Citizens & Ratepayers; not elected.
- **2011:** lost Māngere to William Sio.
- **List MP (May 2013):** replaced Aaron Gilmore as a list MP on 28 May 2013.
- **2014:** withdrew from the election in July, although already selected for Kelston. Chris Penk replaced her as the candidate.

**Roles held:**

- List MP (May 2013–2014)

## Record & notable actions

No significant legislative record in the sources consulted. She was not an MP for the 2013 marriage-equality vote.

## Controversies

- **Charge card (March 2014):** handed back her parliamentary charge card after using it for a Christmas trip to Australia.
- **Employing her wife (April 2014):** breached parliamentary rules by employing her wife in her office. She said she was unaware of the rule and ended the employment.
- **Spending after retiring:** reported to have spent about NZ$23,000 in expenses after announcing she would stand down.

# David Bennett

| | |
|---|---|
| **Party** | New Zealand National Party |
| **Status** | Former MP |
| **Now (Oct 2026)** | Retired at the 2023 election. Appointed to the board of Callaghan Innovation by Judith Collins in 2024; dairy farmer near Te Awamutu. |
| **Electorate(s)** | Hamilton East (2005–2020) |
| **Parliaments** | 48th, 49th, 50th, 51st, 52nd, 53rd |
| **First elected** | 2005 |
| **Born** | 1970-10-28 — Hamilton, New Zealand |
| **Wikipedia** | [David Bennett (New Zealand politician)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bennett_(New_Zealand_politician)) |

## Current status

Former MP. He retired at the 2023 election to spend time with his family. In 2024 Science Minister Judith Collins appointed him to the board of Callaghan Innovation. ([NZ Gazette](https://gazette.govt.nz/notice/id/2024-go1520))

## Biography

- Born 28 October 1970 in Hamilton; attended St John's College.
- LLB and BCA from Victoria University of Wellington.
- Former KPMG accountant. Owns dairy farms near Te Awamutu.
- Formerly in a long-distance relationship with Australian Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie. He is now engaged to Nicky Preston, with whom he has a child.

## Political career

- **Hamilton East:** won the seat from Labour's Dianne Yates in 2005 and held it until 2020, when he lost to Jamie Strange by 2,973 votes. He then returned as a list MP until 2023.
- **Committee chair:** chaired the Transport and Finance select committees.
- **Ministerial roles:** Food Safety, Veterans' Affairs and Racing, outside Cabinet, under Bill English (2016–17). He was the first Hamilton MP to become a minister since 1984.

**Roles held:**

- Minister for Food Safety; Veterans' Affairs; Racing (2016–2017)
- Associate Minister of Transport (2016–2017)
- Chair, Finance and Expenditure Committee (2015–2017); Transport and Industrial Relations Committee (2011–2014)
- Assistant Speaker (2022)
- MP for Hamilton East (2005–2020)
- List MP (2020–2023)

## Record & notable actions

- **Marriage equality:** opposed the bill at first and second readings, then switched to support it at the third reading in 2013. He was the only MP recorded as changing to support.
- **Other conscience votes:**
  - Voted for the abortion bill at every stage.
  - Supported the abortion "safe areas" law and the 2022 conversion-practices ban.
  - Voted against the End of Life Choice Bill (see table).

**Conscience votes** (recorded third-reading votes):

| Bill | Vote |
|---|---|
| [Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill — third reading, 17 Apr 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_(Definition_of_Marriage)_Amendment_Act_2013) | for |
| [End of Life Choice Bill — third reading, 13 Nov 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_Life_Choice_Act_2019) | against |
| [Abortion Legislation Bill — third reading, 18 Mar 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_Legislation_Act_2020) | for |
| Conversion Practices Prohibition Legislation Bill — third reading, 15 Feb 2022 | not among the 8 National MPs recorded as opposed (25 National MPs voted in favour) |

## Controversies

- None of significance recorded in the sources consulted.

- <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bennett_(New_Zealand_politician)>

# Hamish Walker

| | |
|---|---|
| **Party** | New Zealand National Party |
| **Status** | Former MP |
| **Now (Oct 2026)** | Did not stand in 2020 after the COVID-19 patient-data leak. Later worked in Queenstown real estate (Harcourts; then his own firm, since closed). |
| **Electorate(s)** | Clutha-Southland (2017–2020) |
| **Parliaments** | 52nd |
| **First elected** | 2017 |
| **Born** | 1985 — Dunedin, New Zealand |
| **Wikipedia** | [Hamish Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamish_Walker) |

## Current status

Former MP. He did not stand in 2020. He later sold real estate in Queenstown with Harcourts, then founded Premium Real Estate Queenstown, which has since closed.

## Biography

- **Early life:** born in 1985 and raised in Dunedin, where he attended John McGlashan College.
- **Diabetes:** diagnosed at 14.
- **Personal:** his family has roots in Balclutha. His wife, Penny Tipu, is of Māori descent.

## Political career

- **2014:** contested Dunedin South.
- **Clutha-Southland (2017):** a late replacement for Todd Barclay. He won by 14,354 votes.
- **Opposition roles:**
  - Associate agriculture spokesperson (2018–20).
  - Forestry and land information spokesperson (May–July 2020).
- **Local issues:** campaigned to keep Lumsden maternity services.

**Roles held:**

- MP for Clutha-Southland (2017–2020)
- National spokesperson for forestry and land information (May–Jul 2020)

## Record & notable actions

- **Conscience votes:** voted against the End of Life Choice and abortion bills.

**Conscience votes** (recorded third-reading votes):

| Bill | Vote |
|---|---|
| [End of Life Choice Bill — third reading, 13 Nov 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_Life_Choice_Act_2019) | against |
| [Abortion Legislation Bill — third reading, 18 Mar 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_Legislation_Act_2020) | against |

## Controversies

- **Mataura post (Feb 2020):** admitted a social-media post falsely suggesting he had door-knocked in Mataura.
- **Quarantine statement (July 2020):** issued a press release objecting to quarantine facilities for returnees from India, Pakistan and South Korea. Ministers and Dunedin's mayor criticised it as racist "dog whistling", and Todd Muller reprimanded him.
- **Patient-data leak (July 2020):**
  - On 7 July he admitted leaking COVID-19 patient details to media, information he had received from former party president Michelle Boag. ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300051710/national-mp-hamish-walker-admits-passing-on-leaked-covid19-patient-info-from-former-party-president-michelle-boag))
  - He was stripped of his portfolios, and Muller asked the party board to expel him. Walker announced he would not stand again. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/420754/covid-19-privacy-leak-mp-hamish-walker-announces-he-won-t-stand-for-re-election))
  - Michael Heron QC's inquiry found his actions were politically motivated and "not justified or reasonable".

## Sources

His earlier roles were chair of ANZ Bank New Zealand (from 2017) and Air New Zealand director (2017–2020). He was knighted (GNZM) in 2017. In 2026 he publicly backed his friend Christopher Luxon amid leadership speculation and was reported to be advising him. In September 2025 he attended Beijing's Victory Day parade with Helen Clark and met Xi Jinping. ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/business/crimson-education-names-sir-john-key-as-chairman-hints-at-ipo-more-acquisitions/premium/EEELXVKM6REZDLXM7DTJ73IFOA/)) ## Biography - **Early life:** - Born 9 August 1961 in Auckland. - His father, an English immigrant and war veteran, died when John was eight. He was estimated to be worth about US$35m in 2016. - **Family:** married to Bronagh; two children. ## Political career - **Helensville:** won the new seat in 2002, National's worst-ever election, by 1,705 votes. Bill English succeeded him. Key left Parliament on 14 April 2017. ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2016/dec/05/john-key-resigns-new-zealand-prime-minister-to-quit)) **Roles held:** - Prime Minister of New Zealand (2008–2016) - Leader of the National Party (2006–2016) - Leader of the Opposition (2006–2008) - Minister of Tourism (2008–2016) - Minister of National Security and Intelligence (2014–2016) - Minister Responsible for the GCSB and NZSIS (2008–2014) - National finance spokesperson (2004–2006) - Chairman, International Democrat Union (2014–2018) - MP for Helensville (2002–2017) ## Record & notable actions - **Economy:** - Personal tax cuts (top rate cut to 33%) and a rise in GST from 12.5% to 15% in 2010, despite earlier saying GST would not rise. - Spending restraint during the GFC. - Partial sale of five state-owned enterprises (the "mixed ownership model"). Voters opposed this about 2:1 in a citizens-initiated referendum. - **Christchurch earthquakes:** set up CERA after the February 2011 quake, which killed 185 people. - **Foreign policy:** - Signed the Wellington Declaration with the US (2010). - Led New Zealand's successful 2015–16 UN Security Council campaign. - Withdrew troops from Afghanistan. - Championed the TPP, signed in Auckland in February 2016. - Won a citizenship pathway for New Zealanders in Australia (2016). - **Other:** - National Cycleway (Ngā Haerenga). - The 2015–16 flag referendums, in which voters kept the current flag. # Mike Sabin

| | |
|---|---|
| **Party** | New Zealand National Party |
| **Status** | Former MP |
| **Now (Oct 2026)** | Resigned from Parliament on 30 January 2015 'due to personal issues'; later reported working at Peppers Carrington Resort, Karikari (2015). Current activities not verified. |
| **Electorate(s)** | Northland (2011–2015) |
| **Parliaments** | 50th, 51st |
| **First elected** | 2011 |
| **Born** | 1968-09-24 |
| **Wikipedia** | [Mike Sabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Sabin) |

## Current status

Former MP. He resigned on 30 January 2015, which triggered the 2015 Northland by-election; Winston Peters won it. In 2015 he was reported to be working at Peppers Carrington Resort in Karikari. His current activities are not verified.

## Biography

- **Early life:** born on 24 September 1968 and raised in Whangārei.
- **Navy and dairy:** seaman officer in the RNZ Navy in the 1980s, then worked in the dairy industry.
- **Police and drug education:**
  - Police officer from the 1990s.
  - Founded the drug-education company MethCon (2006; sold 2010).
  - Helped bring about the Alcohol and Other Drug Treatment Court.
  - Received a Sir Peter Blake Emerging Leader Award (2008).
- **Personal:** father of journalist Brook Sabin. He wrote *The Long Way Home*, about his son Darryl's rugby brain injury.

## Political career

- **Northland:** succeeded John Carter, winning by 11,362 votes in 2011 and 9,300 in 2014.
- **Ministerial prospects:** John Key later said he had considered making Sabin a minister after the 2014 election.

**Roles held:**

- MP for Northland (2011–2015)

## Record & notable actions

- **Conscience votes:** voted against marriage equality (2013).

**Conscience votes** (recorded third-reading votes):

| Bill | Vote |
|---|---|
| [Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill — third reading, 17 Apr 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_(Definition_of_Marriage)_Amendment_Act_2013) | against |

## Controversies

- **Resignation (January 2015):** in December 2014 media reported he was under police investigation over an assault complaint. Police, Key and Sabin did not confirm the reports at the time. He resigned with immediate effect, citing personal issues "best dealt with outside Parliament".

## Sources

- <http://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA1501/S00163/mike-sabin-announces-resignation-as-northland-mp.htm>

A dairy farmer near Levin, who studied farming at Massey University and took over his father's farm. - Horowhenua district councillor (1998–2005). - Comes from a local-government family: his father, Malcolm Guy, was the first Mayor of Horowhenua. ## Political career - **Ōtaki:** lost the seat to Labour's Darren Hughes by 382 votes in 2005 and entered Parliament on the list. He won Ōtaki in 2008 and held it until 2020. - **Whip:** junior and then senior whip. - **Ministerial career:** - Minister of Internal Affairs (from June 2009), during which he merged the National Library and Archives NZ into the DIA. - Immigration, Racing and Veterans' Affairs (2011–13). - Primary Industries (2013–17), including the response to the 2013 Fonterra botulism scare. - **Retirement:** announced in July 2019. ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/rural/2019/07/national-party-reshuffle-after-nathan-guy-announces-retirement-from-politics.html)) **Roles held:** - Minister for Primary Industries (2013–2017) - Minister of Immigration (2011–2013) - Minister for Racing; Veterans' Affairs (2011–2013) - Minister of Internal Affairs (2009–2011) - National senior whip (2008–2009); junior whip (2006–2008) - National agriculture spokesperson (2018–2019) - MP for Ōtaki (2008–2020) - List MP (2005–2008) - Horowhenua District Councillor (1998–2005) ## Record & notable actions - **Conscience votes:** voted against marriage equality, End of Life Choice and abortion reform (see table). **Conscience votes** (recorded third-reading votes): | Bill | Vote | |---|---| | [Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill — third reading, 17 Apr 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_(Definition_of_Marriage)_Amendment_Act_2013) | against | | [End of Life Choice Bill — third reading, 13 Nov 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_Life_Choice_Act_2019) | against | | [Abortion Legislation Bill — third reading, 18 Mar 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_Legislation_Act_2020) | against | ## Controversies - **Peter Thiel citizenship (revealed 2017):** as Internal Affairs Minister in 2011, he granted citizenship to US billionaire Peter Thiel under "exceptional circumstances" after only 12 days' residence. Thiel was the first adult granted citizenship without meeting the residency requirement. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/326696/thiel's-nz-citizenship-one-of-a-kind)) ## Sources - - - - - Photo: — Office of Nathan Guy. — Sent and authorised by Phil Rennie, Private Secretary to Hon. Nathan Guy. (CC0)
parties/national/people/nick-smith/READM: # Nick Smith | | | |---|---| | **Party** | New Zealand National Party | | **Status** | Former MP | | **Now (Oct 2026)** | Mayor of Nelson (elected Oct 2022; re-elected Oct 2025). Left Parliament 10 June 2021. | | **Electorate(s)** | Tasman (1990–1996); Nelson (1996–2020) | | **Parliaments** | 43th, 44th, 45th, 46th, 47th, 48th, 49th, 50th, 51st, 52nd, 53rd | | **First elected** | 1990 | | **Born** | 1964-12-24 — Rangiora, Canterbury Region, New Zealand | | **Wikipedia** | [Nick Smith (New Zealand politician)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Smith_(New_Zealand_politician)) | ## Current status Mayor of Nelson. He was first elected in October 2022, beating Matt Lawrey by 9,302 votes, and re-elected in October 2025. He left Parliament on 10 June 2021. ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/nelson-mail/300708404/new-nelson-mayor-nick-smith-gets-down-to-business), [Nelson City Council](https://www.nelson.govt.nz/1your-council/elected-members-mayor-and-councillors)) ## Biography - Born 24 December 1964 in Rangiora, into a family of construction contractors. - Studied at the University of Canterbury: BE (Hons) in civil engineering and a PhD on soil strength and landslide stability. - Worked as an engineer and as a director of the family firm. - Elected to Rangiora District Council at 21. ## Political career - **Electorates:** - MP for Tasman, 1990–96. - MP for Nelson, 1996–2020. - Lost Nelson to Rachel Boyack in 2020 and returned as a list MP. ([Electoral Commission](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-27.html)) - **Cabinet, 1996–99:** Conservation (after the Cave Creek disaster), Corrections, then Education. - **Deputy leadership, 2003:** deputy leader for under three weeks under Don Brash. He lost the post to Gerry Brownlee while on stress leave. - **Fifth National Government:** - Environment, Climate Change and ACC (from 2008). - Resigned all portfolios in March 2012 over the ACC letter (see Controversies). - Returned in 2013 in Conservation and Housing. - Building and Housing and Environment, 2014–17. - **Father of the House** from 2018 until he left Parliament. **Roles held:** - Mayor of Nelson (2022–) - Minister for the Environment (2008–2012, 2014–2017) - Minister for Climate Change Issues (2008–2011) - Minister for ACC (2008–2012) - Minister of Building and Housing (2013–2017) - Minister of Conservation (1996–1999, 2013–2014) - Minister of Local Government (2010–2011) - Minister of Education (1999) - Minister of Corrections (1997–1999) - Deputy Leader of the National Party (Oct–Nov 2003) - Father of the House (2018–2021) - MP for Tasman (1990–1996) - MP for Nelson (1996–2020) - List MP (2020–2021) ## Record & notable actions - **Emissions trading:** led National's 2009 amendments to the Emissions Trading Scheme. - **Environment Canterbury (2010):** replaced the elected regional council with government-appointed commissioners. At the time, his brother's company was facing charges from that council. ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/the-press/3613819/Last-rites-for-ECan)) - **Housing and building:** Minister of Building and Housing during the mid-2010s housing crisis. - **Electoral law:** in 2021 he sponsored a member's bill to repeal the "waka-jumping" Electoral (Integrity) Amendment Act. It was defeated 65–55. - **Conscience votes:** voted against marriage equality, End of Life Choice and abortion reform (see table). **Conscience votes** (recorded third-reading votes): | Bill | Vote | |---|---| | [Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill — third reading, 17 Apr 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_(Definition_of_Marriage)_Amendment_Act_2013) | against | | [End of Life Choice Bill — third reading, 13 Nov 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_Life_Choice_Act_2019) | against | | [Abortion Legislation Bill — third reading, 18 Mar 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_Legislation_Act_2020) | against | ## Controversies - **Contempt of court (2004):** found guilty of contempt over comments he made about a constituent's Family Court case. - **Defamation (2010):** settled the Osmose defamation case with an apology. Taxpayer funding of his legal costs in other cases drew scrutiny. - **ACC letter (2012):** resigned from Cabinet after writing on ministerial letterhead in support of a friend's ACC claim (the Bronwyn Pullar case). ([RNZ](http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/political/101387/smith-resigns-portfolios-over-acc-letter)) - **Ejection from the House (2020):** escorted out by the Serjeant-at-Arms, the first MP removed that way since Muldoon, after calling Parliament a "Nazi establishment". ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/419892/national-mp-nick-smith-booted-from-the-house-calls-govt-nazi-establishment)) - **Resignation (2021):** left Parliament while a Parliamentary Service inquiry into a 2020 "verbal altercation" in his office was under way. ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300322387/nick-smith-resignation-audio-recording-of-verbal-altercation-at-centre-of-dispute)) ## Sources - - - - - - - - - Photo: — David Hollander — https://livingheritage.lincoln.ac.nz/nodes/view/11961 (CC BY-SA 3.0 nz)

parties/national/people/nicola-grigg/REA: # Nicola Grigg | | | |---|---| | **Party** | New Zealand National Party | | **Status** | Current MP — standing in 2026 | | **Now (Oct 2026)** | Minister for the Environment (since 7 Apr 2026), Minister for Women, Minister of State for Trade and Investment and Associate Minister of Agriculture/ACC; MP for Selwyn; #16 on National's 2026 list and re-contesting Selwyn. | | **Electorate(s)** | Selwyn (2020–) | | **Parliaments** | 53rd, 54th | | **First elected** | 2020 | | **2026 election** | list #16, standing in Selwyn | | **Wikipedia** | [Nicola Grigg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicola_Grigg) | > **List rank note:** policy.nz (in the 2026 candidacy section below) gives #17. The Electoral Commission's official National list gives **#16**. From #14 down, policy.nz's numbering appears to still include Chris Penk, who withdrew. ([Electoral Commission](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/party-lists)) ## Current status Minister for the Environment since the 2 April 2026 reshuffle. She also holds Minister for Women and Minister of State for Trade and Investment, both since November 2023, and associate roles in Agriculture and ACC. She is MP for Selwyn and #16 on National's 2026 list. ## Biography - **Early life:** born and raised in Mount Somers, Mid Canterbury. - **Family:** her great-grandparents Arthur Grigg and Mary Grigg were both MPs for Mid-Canterbury. Mary Grigg, who completed Arthur's term after his death, was National's first woman MP. She is also descended from Premier Sir John Hall. - **Career:** - Journalist at Newstalk ZB and RNZ. - Press secretary and adviser to Bill English (as finance minister and Prime Minister) and to Simon Bridges. - Worked at New Zealand Trade and Enterprise. - **Personal:** lives in Prebbleton with her partner Phil. They have a son, born around the end of 2023 (she announced the pregnancy in October 2023). ## Political career - **Selection:** chosen in November 2019 on the first ballot for Selwyn, described as National's safest seat. ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/117306482/national-puts-former-journalist-nicola-grigg-forward-for-safest-seat-in-nz)) - **Elections:** won Selwyn by 4,968 votes in 2020 and by 19,782 in 2023. ([Electoral Commission](https://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-45.html)) - **Opposition spokesperson:** women; trade and export growth; then rural communities, animal welfare, biosecurity and food safety. - **Ministerial appointments:** became a minister outside Cabinet on 27 November 2023. Environment was added in April 2026. **Roles held:** - Minister for the Environment (2026–) - Minister for Women (2023–) - Minister of State for Trade and Investment (2023–) - Associate Minister of Agriculture (2023–) - Associate Minister for ACC - National spokesperson for women; trade and export growth; rural communities, animal welfare, biosecurity (2020–2023) - MP for Selwyn (2020–) ## Record & notable actions - **Trade:** represented New Zealand at ASEAN economic ministers' meetings (2024), PACER Plus (2024) and the Pacific Islands Forum trade ministers' meeting (2025). She also joined prime ministerial trade missions. - **Women:** launched a gender pay-gap toolkit, the "Free to Lead" online-harm toolkit and the BoardConnector governance database. ([Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/pay-gap-calculator-toolkit-launched)) - **Environment:** introduced the Hazardous Substances and New Organisms Amendment Bill (May 2026), intended to streamline HSNO approvals. ([Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/amendment-proposed-streamline-hazardous-substance-and-new-organism-approvals)) - **Positions:** supported the 2022 abortion "safe areas" law, arguing it would reduce harassment of women. ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2021/03/how-mps-voted-on-law-change-that-would-allow-safe-zones-around-abortion-clinics.html)) - **Conscience votes:** she was in Parliament for the 2022 conversion-practices vote and was not among the eight National MPs recorded as opposed. ## Controversies - None recorded in the sources consulted. ## 2026 candidacy - **Electorate:** Selwyn - **List ranking:** 17 _Source: candidate questionnaire answers published on [policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/national-party), retrieved Oct 2026._ ## Sources - - - - - - - - - - - - - Photo: — Supplied to policy.nz by the candidate/party (Not stated (candidate photo supplied to policy.nz; used for identification))
parties/national/people/nicola-willis/RE: # Nicola Willis | | | |---|---| | **Party** | New Zealand National Party | | **Status** | Current MP — standing in 2026 | | **Now (Oct 2026)** | Minister of Finance, Minister for Economic Growth and Minister for Social Investment; Deputy Leader of the National Party (since 2021). List MP; #2 on National's 2026 list (list-only — no electorate candidacy). | | **Parliaments** | 52nd, 53rd, 54th | | **First elected** | 2018 | | **Born** | 1981-03-07 — Wellington, New Zealand | | **2026 election** | list #2 | | **Wikipedia** | [Nicola Willis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicola_Willis) | ## Current status Minister of Finance since 27 November 2023, and also Minister for Economic Growth (since January 2025) and Minister for Social Investment. She has been deputy leader of the National Party since 30 November 2021. She is a list MP and is #2 on National's 2026 list without an electorate candidacy. She delivered Budget 2026 in late May 2026, forecasting a return to surplus (OBEGALx) by 2028/29 and ruling out "election-year band-aids and sugar hits". ([Treasury](https://www.treasury.govt.nz/publications/budget-speech/budget-speech-2026), [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/596610/budget-2026-at-a-glance-the-big-changes-winners-and-losers-what-you-need-to-know)) ## Biography - **Early life and education:** - Born on 7 March 1981 in Wellington and grew up in Point Howard, Lower Hutt. - Her mother was a Press Gallery journalist and her father a Bell Gully partner. Her great-great-grandfather Archibald Willis was a Liberal MP in the 1890s–1900s. - Attended Samuel Marsden Collegiate and King's College (Auckland). - Studied English literature at Victoria University of Wellington (first-class honours) and took a postgraduate journalism diploma at Canterbury. - **Early career:** research and policy adviser to Bill English, then senior adviser to John Key in 2008. During 2008 debate preparation she played Helen Clark. - **Business career:** - From 2012, government-relations manager and later general manager at Fonterra. - Board member of ExportNZ. - Director of the New Zealand Initiative (2016–17). - **Personal:** married to Duncan Small; four children. ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/nicola-willis-at-home-who-is-nationals-new-deputy-leader-away-from-the-spotlight/C6R64EEY4CBSIOVW7BN5TETTTE/)) ## Political career - **2017 election:** contested Wellington Central and lost to Grant Robertson, taking about 26% of the electorate vote. She was #48 on the list and just missed out on the final count. - **3 April 2018:** entered Parliament from the list when Steven Joyce resigned. She was spokesperson for early childhood education. - **2020 leadership change:** worked as a "numbers" organiser, with Chris Bishop, in Todd Muller's successful challenge to Simon Bridges. She became housing spokesperson, and then education spokesperson under Judith Collins. - **2020 election:** lost Wellington Central again and returned on the list. As housing spokesperson she worked with Labour's Megan Woods on the cross-party Medium Density Residential Standards (2021). - **30 Nov 2021:** elected deputy leader unopposed as Christopher Luxon's running mate. She became finance spokesperson in March 2022 when Bridges resigned. - **2023 election:** lost Ōhāriu to Labour's Greg O'Connor by 1,260 votes; returned on the list. ([Electoral Commission](https://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-33.html)) - **Ministerial appointments:** - 27 Nov 2023: Finance, Public Service, Social Investment, Associate Climate Change. - January 2025: became the first Minister for Economic Growth and gave up the Public Service portfolio. **Roles held:** - Minister of Finance (2023–) - Minister for Social Investment (2023–) - Minister for Economic Growth (2025–) - Minister for the Public Service (2023–2025) - Associate Minister of Climate Change (2023–) - Acting Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs (Grocery Sector) (2025) - Deputy Leader of the National Party (2021–) - Deputy Leader of the Opposition (2021–2023) - National finance spokesperson (2022–2023) - National housing spokesperson (2020–2022) - National education spokesperson (2020) - List MP (2018–) ## Record & notable actions - **Fiscal stance:** - Mini-budget (20 Dec 2023): NZ$7.47b of claimed operating savings. - Budget 2024: about NZ$14b of personal income-tax relief, partly funded by public-service savings and programme cuts. - Budget 2025: reduced the new-spending allowance to NZ$1.3b and dropped the planned Digital Services Tax. - Budget 2026: focused on returning to surplus. - Treasury forecasts (Dec 2024) showed deficits until at least 2029. She adopted the OBEGALx measure, which excludes ACC, as the headline target. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/536933/hyefu-revealed-nicola-willis-deploys-convenient-new-measure-amid-bleak-books)) - **Interislander ferries:** - In December 2023 she declined KiwiRail's request for NZ$1.47b more for the iReX project, which ended it. Cancellation costs were put at about NZ$300m. - A replacement procurement through a new company was announced in December 2024, with new ships expected around 2029. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/504650/interislander-ferry-fleet-project-to-wind-down-after-being-denied-further-government-funding)) - **Cost of living and competition:** - Budget 2024 raised the Working for Families in-work tax credit, worth up to NZ$50 a fortnight for about 160,000 families. - Announced an "express lane" consenting regime (2025) to bring new supermarket competitors in. - In 2026 accused Foodstuffs and Woolworths of a "full-court press" lobbying campaign against reforms to break up the duopoly. ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2025/08/27/express-lane-reforms-to-increase-supermarket-competition-willis/)) - **Other decisions:** - Smallest minimum-wage rise since the 1990s, to NZ$23.50 (Dec 2024). - Guidance that public-service working from home is "not an entitlement" (Sept 2024). - Proposed relaxing government procurement rules, including the Living Wage requirement for cleaning and security contracts. - Announced a review of the Reserve Bank's COVID-era monetary policy (Feb 2026). - **Member's bill:** her 2023 bill to let parents share paid parental leave and take it at the same time was blocked by Labour at first reading. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/495025/labour-blocks-national-s-paid-parental-leave-bill-that-would-have-allowed-parents-to-share-time-off)) - **Positions:** - Described as a social liberal and a member of National's BlueGreens caucus. - Voted for the End of Life Choice and Abortion Legislation bills (see table). - Supported Labour's Equal Pay Amendment in 2018, but in 2025 backed the government bill restricting pay-equity claims, while calling herself a feminist. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/560142/pay-equity-changes-two-sides-of-the-coalition-brought-out)) **Conscience votes** (recorded third-reading votes): | Bill | Vote | |---|---| | [End of Life Choice Bill — third reading, 13 Nov 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_Life_Choice_Act_2019) | for | | [Abortion Legislation Bill — third reading, 18 Mar 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_Legislation_Act_2020) | for | | Conversion Practices Prohibition Legislation Bill — third reading, 15 Feb 2022 | not among the 8 National MPs recorded as opposed (25 National MPs voted in favour) | ## Controversies - **"$250 a fortnight" tax promise (2023):** - She admitted that only about 3,000 households would receive the full NZ$250 a fortnight. - She said she would resign if the tax plan was not delivered. - The foreign-buyer tax meant to help fund it was dropped in coalition talks. ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/09/15/nicola-willis-id-quit-as-finance-minister-if-my-tax-cut-plan-fails/), [Newsroom](https://newsroom.co.nz/2023/11/24/which-policies-survived-the-negotiations-and-which-didnt/)) - **Cancer medicines (Budget 2024):** National's election promise to fund 13 cancer drugs was not met in Budget 2024. The government blamed a NZ$1.77b Pharmac funding "cliff" left by its predecessor, and Willis said the government would seek funding later. In June 2024 the government announced NZ$604m over four years for Pharmac to fund 54 medicines, including 26 cancer treatments, which it said fulfilled the promise ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/520419/cancer-drugs-promise-government-confirms-600m-extra-for-pharmac)). ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2024/05/budget-2024-finance-minister-nicola-willis-defends-national-u-turn-on-funding-new-cancer-drugs.html)) - **Criticism of economic management:** - Open letters from 15 economists (Nov 2024) and 20 economists (Oct 2025) blamed fiscal restraint for prolonging the recession. Willis replied that she did not agree. - After a 0.9% GDP fall in the June 2025 quarter, Sir Roger Douglas and economist Robert MacCulloch called for her resignation. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/573459/former-finance-minister-sir-roger-douglas-calls-for-finance-minister-nicola-willis-to-resign)) - From the right, the Taxpayers' Union ran a "Nicola Fudge Co." campaign in December 2025. Willis challenged its chair, Ruth Richardson, to a debate, which did not go ahead. ## 2026 candidacy - **List ranking:** 2 _Source: candidate questionnaire answers published on [policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/national-party), retrieved Oct 2026._ ## Sources - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - Photo: — Supplied to policy.nz by the candidate/party (Not stated (candidate photo supplied to policy.nz; used for identification))
parties/national/people/nikki-kaye/READM: # Nikki Kaye | | | |---|---| | **Party** | New Zealand National Party | | **Status** | Deceased (former MP) | | **Now (Oct 2026)** | Died of breast cancer on 23 November 2024, aged 44. Left Parliament at the 2020 election. | | **Electorate(s)** | Auckland Central (2008–2020) | | **Parliaments** | 49th, 50th, 51st, 52nd | | **First elected** | 2008 | | **Born** | 1980-02-11 — Auckland, New Zealand | | **Died** | 2024-11-23 | | **Wikipedia** | [Nikki Kaye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikki_Kaye) | ## Current status Deceased. Nikki Kaye died of breast cancer on 23 November 2024, aged 44. She had left Parliament at the 2020 election. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/534834/former-national-party-minister-nikki-kaye-dies-aged-44)) ## Biography - **Early life:** born Nicola Laura Kaye on 11 February 1980 in Auckland, and grew up in Epsom and Kohimarama. She was head prefect at Corran School. - **Education:** genetics degree from the University of Otago and a law degree completed in Wellington. - **Athlete:** Auckland women's 3,000m champion (1997). The Electoral Commission's official National list gives **#14**. From #14 down, policy.nz's numbering appears to still include Chris Penk, who withdrew. ([Electoral Commission](https://vote.nz/2026-general-election/voting-in-the-election/party-lists)) ## Current status Since the 2 April 2026 reshuffle she has been in Cabinet as Minister for Tertiary Education and Minister of Science, Innovation and Technology. She handed the Environment portfolio, which she held from 2023, to Nicola Grigg. She is MP for Invercargill and is #14 on National's official 2026 list (shown as #15 in policy.nz's earlier list). ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/04/02/christopher-luxon-reveals-cabinet-shake-up/), [Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/pm-refreshes-ministerial-team)) ## Biography - **Early life:** born in September 1959 in Southland and grew up in Riversdale and Te Tipua. She attended Gore High School and has a BSc from the University of Otago. She served several years in the Territorial Force. - **Southern Institute of Technology:** chief executive from 1997 to 2020. She introduced SIT's Zero Fees Scheme. - **Other roles:** director of the Southland Museum and Art Gallery, Southland DHB board member and Woolf Fisher Fellow (2000). - **Honours:** CNZM for services to education, sport and the community (2016). - **Personal:** married with three daughters. ## Political career - **2020:** chosen for Invercargill after Sarah Dowie retired. She narrowly held the seat for National, beating Labour's Liz Craig by 224 votes, while Labour won most regional seats. ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/123320312/penny-simmonds-takes-invercargill-electorate-seat)) - **In opposition:** tertiary education spokesperson and a strong critic of the Te Pūkenga polytechnic merger. She also voted against the 2021 COVID vaccination mandate law and the 2022 abortion "safe areas" law. - **2023:** held Invercargill by 10,945 votes. She became Minister for Disability Issues, the Environment, and Tertiary Education and Skills, and Associate Social Development and Employment, all outside Cabinet. **Roles held:** - Minister of Science, Innovation and Technology (2026–) - Minister for Tertiary Education (and Skills) (2023–) - Minister for the Environment (2023–2026) - Minister for Disability Issues (2023–2024) - Associate Minister for Social Development and Employment (2023–) - National spokesperson for tertiary education; workforce planning (2020–2023) - MP for Invercargill (2020–) - Chief executive, Southern Institute of Technology (1997–2020) ## Record & notable actions - **Te Pūkenga:** - Led the break-up of the national polytechnic Te Pūkenga. - Ten polytechnics regained regional governance from 1 January 2026. Others are to join a federation or await viability decisions, and Te Pūkenga is to be dissolved by 31 December 2026. - Workforce Development Councils are being replaced by Industry Skills Boards. ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/te-pukenga-government-restores-regional-governance-for-10-polytechnics-unwinds-merger/PTO27FLB3VBTNJVYWLIGJIU35Q/), [Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/regional-governance-will-return-ten-polytechnics)) - **Free speech:** with David Seymour, proposed strengthening universities' free-speech obligations (December 2024). ([Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/strengthening-free-speech-universities)) - **Environment (2023–26):** Minister for the Environment outside Cabinet until April 2026. Her decisions in that portfolio are not covered in the sources used for this profile. ## Controversies - **Disability funding (March 2024):** ([RNZ: "we got it wrong"](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/512172/we-got-it-wrong-on-disability-announcement-minister-penny-simmonds)) - Whaikaha suddenly tightened what families could spend flexible respite funding on. - Simmonds said the government's "coffers are not an endless open pit" and suggested some families were spending funding on "massages, overseas travel and pedicures". This caused an outcry, including a petition with more than 10,000 signatures in 24 hours. - Finance Minister Willis called officials in, and Cabinet took tighter control of the ministry. ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/350218178/parents-worried-their-children-will-suffer-disability-services-suddenly-cut), [Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/350219245/finance-minister-nicola-willis-calls-officials-after-cuts-disability-services)) - On 24 April 2024 Luxon removed her from Disability Issues. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/515100/media-minister-melissa-lee-demoted-from-cabinet-penny-simmonds-stripped-of-portfolio)) - **2020 election night:** Mayor Tim Shadbolt was criticised for listing her election-night party as an official mayoral engagement. ## 2026 candidacy - **Electorate:** Invercargill - **List ranking:** 15 _Source: candidate questionnaire answers published on [policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/national-party), retrieved Oct 2026._ ## Sources - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - Photo: — Supplied to policy.nz by the candidate/party (Not stated (candidate photo supplied to policy.nz; used for identification))

| | |
|---|---|
