## Current status

Former MP. He retired at the 2014 election and returned to his central North Island farms. Barbara Kuriger succeeded him.

## Biography

- **Early life:** born on 26 January 1960 and raised in Ōpunake.
- **Farming:** a dairy farmer.
- **Family:** a distant cousin of Jacinda Ardern.

## Political career

- **Taranaki-King Country (1998):** won the by-election that followed Jim Bolger's retirement, and held the seat until 2014.
- **Committee chair:** Primary Production Committee (2008–14).

**Roles held:**

- MP for Taranaki-King Country (1998–2014)
- Chair, Primary Production Committee (2008–2014)

## Record & notable actions

- **Fonterra:** a driving force behind the 2001 legislation that created Fonterra.
- **Conscience votes:** voted against marriage equality (2013).

**Conscience votes** (recorded third-reading votes):

| Bill | Vote |
|---|---|
| [Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill — third reading, 17 Apr 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_(Definition_of_Marriage)_Amendment_Act_2013) | against |

## Controversies

- **Tractor protest (2003):** drove a tractor up Parliament's steps to protest the proposed agricultural emissions research levy, the "fart tax". He was charged with disorderly conduct; police withdrew the charge after a judge called the case a waste of resources.

parties/national/people/tama-potaka/READ: # Tama Potaka | | | |---|---| | **Party** | New Zealand National Party | | **Status** | Current MP — standing in 2026 | | **Now (Oct 2026)** | Minister of Conservation, Minister for Māori Development, Minister for Māori Crown Relations: Te Arawhiti, Minister for Whānau Ora and Associate Minister of Housing (Social Housing); MP for Hamilton West; #11 on National's 2026 list and re-contesting Hamilton West. | | **Electorate(s)** | Hamilton West (2022–) | | **Parliaments** | 53rd, 54th | | **First elected** | 2022 | | **Born** | 1976-01-08 — Raetihi, New Zealand | | **2026 election** | list #11, standing in Hamilton West | | **Wikipedia** | [Tama Potaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tama_Potaka) | ## Current status Minister of Conservation, Māori Development, Māori Crown Relations: Te Arawhiti, and Whānau Ora, and Associate Minister of Housing (Social Housing), since November 2023. He affiliates to Ngāti Hauiti, Whanganui, Taranaki and Ngāti Toa. - **Education:** - Dux of Te Aute College (1993). - BA/LLB from Victoria University of Wellington (1999). - LLM from Columbia University on a scholarship. - Graduate of Te Panekiretanga o Te Reo Māori. - **Legal career:** - Attorney at Simpson Thacher & Bartlett in New York. - Later at Rudd Watts & Stone and Bell Gully, and in public-policy roles. - **Business and iwi roles:** - General manager of corporate services at Tainui Group Holdings (about seven years, Hamilton). - Senior adviser at the NZ Superannuation Fund. - Chief executive of Ngāi Tai ki Tāmaki Trust from 2020. - A lead negotiator for the Mōkai Pātea Treaty claim (2021). - **Personal:** married to Ariana Paul (2008); three children. ## Political career - **2022 Hamilton West by-election:** held after Gaurav Sharma resigned. He held Hamilton West at the 2023 election by 6,488 votes. ([Electoral Commission](https://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-13.html)) **Roles held:** - Minister of Conservation (2023–) - Minister for Māori Development (2023–) - Minister for Māori Crown Relations: Te Arawhiti (2023–) - Minister for Whānau Ora (2023–) - Associate Minister of Housing (Social Housing) (2023–) - National spokesperson for Māori development (2023) - MP for Hamilton West (2022–) ## Record & notable actions **Māori–Crown relations** - Met Kīngi Tūheitia with Luxon (January 2024) and attended the King's national unity hui. - Moved Te Arawhiti's Treaty-settlement monitoring functions to Te Puni Kōkiri (August 2024). Opposition parties called it a backward step. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te-manu-korihi/525032/government-clarifying-functions-of-te-arawhiti-and-te-puni-kokiri)) - Overhauled the Waitangi Tribunal's membership (January 2025), with eight new members including Ron Mark. Te Pāti Māori called it a "whitewash"; Potaka rejected that. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/te-manu-korihi/539260/minister-overhauls-waitangi-tribunal-membership)) - Set up a technical advisory group to review the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, as required by the coalition agreements. ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/waitangi-tribunal-review-to-kick-off-this-year-government-confirms-act-calls-it-activist/26L35ZWBDFCFPNMHQG4ONDTRMA/)) - Member of the ministerial group reviewing Treaty clauses in legislation (see Paul Goldsmith). **Conservation** - Raised the International Visitor Levy from NZ$35 to NZ$100 (from October 2024). - Announced 19 new marine protection areas in the Hauraki Gulf. - Added feral cats to Predator Free 2050 (November 2025). ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/579503/stone-cold-killer-feral-cats-added-to-predator-free-2050-strategy-conservation-minister-announces)) - Planned charges for foreign visitors at four premium natural sites. ([Euronews](https://www.euronews.com/travel/2025/08/05/new-zealand-to-charge-foreign-tourists-to-visit-four-of-its-most-famous-natural-attraction)) - Sponsored the Conservation Amendment Bill (first reading 13 May 2026, 68–54). After criticism, he withdrew its land disposal and exchange clauses in June 2026. ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/minister-tama-potaka-to-remove-controversial-disposal-and-exchange-clauses-from-conservation-act/BGHOZIKFXBCZZNNSM4Q3YYCD5E/)) **Social housing** - Tightened eligibility for emergency housing. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/526461/what-you-need-to-know-about-the-new-rules-tightening-the-gateway-into-emergency-housing)) - Households in emergency-housing motels fell from 3,141 (December 2023) to 591 (December 2024). The government said it had met its target five years early, but could not account for about 20% of those who left. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/539858/government-says-it-s-hit-emergency-housing-target-5-years-early)) - Announced a programme of 189 social and affordable homes in Rotorua (2025) and the closure of the city's emergency-housing motels. **Other** - In 2023 he publicly disagreed with Simeon Brown's view that road signs should be English-only. ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2023/05/national-s-tama-potaka-takes-simeon-brown-for-korero-over-te-reo-road-signs-as-m-ori-mps-break-party-line.html)) - He was not in Parliament for the 2013–2022 conscience votes. ## Controversies - **Criticism of government Māori policy:** opposition parties and Māori leaders have criticised the government's policies on Māori, which he has defended as minister. Standing again in Waiariki in 2026; Te Pāti Māori is campaigning for electorate votes only (its 2026 list contains only general secretary Lance Norman) and urging supporters to party-vote Labour or Green. In 2025–26 the party went through a bitter internal split that saw MPs Mariameno Kapa-Kingi and Tākuta Ferris expelled (Kapa-Kingi was reinstated by the High Court before forming her own party). ## Biography Rawiri Wikuki Waititi was born in Ōpōtiki on 17 October (c. 1980) and raised at Whangaparāoa near Cape Runaway in Te Whānau-ā-Apanui, attending kōhanga reo and kura kaupapa before moving to West Auckland at 13 (Rutherford High School). Married to Kiri Tamihere-Waititi (daughter of party president John Tamihere); five children. ## Political career - Labour candidate for Waiariki in 2014 (lost to Te Ururoa Flavell); switched to the Māori Party in 2016. - Won **Waiariki** in 2020 by 836 votes over Labour's Tāmati Coffey, returning the party to Parliament (and bringing in Ngarewa-Packer on the list); confirmed male co-leader on 28 October 2020, replacing John Tamihere. - Re-elected in 2023 with an outright majority (21,500 of 28,958 votes). ## Record & notable actions - Helped negotiate the end of the 2020–21 Waikeria Prison rooftop protest at the inmates' request. - His 2021 refusal to wear a tie ("a colonial noose") led to his ejection and then to Parliament dropping the tie requirement. - Member's bill to remove GST from food (defeated at first reading March 2024, supported only by TPM). - With Ngarewa-Packer proposed a Parliamentary Commissioner for Te Tiriti with a "Tiriti veto" (February 2025); advocates a Māori Parliament, a wealth tax and foreign-policy neutrality ("Switzerland of the South Pacific"). - Voted for the conversion-practices ban (2022) and abortion safe-areas law (2022); against the one-off Queen Elizabeth II Memorial Day holiday (2022). ## Controversies - **Treaty Principles Bill haka (14 November 2024):** with Maipi-Clarke, Ngarewa-Packer and Labour's Peeni Henare performed a protest haka that disrupted the bill's first-reading vote. An RNZ-Reid Research poll found 54% thought the punishment about right or too lenient, 36% too harsh. - **Suppression breach (August 2023):** suspended for 24 hours for referring to suppressed court proceedings under privilege; the Privileges Committee upheld the action. - Joked at a July 2023 party conference about putting karaka berries in David Seymour's water; Seymour demanded an apology. - Defended the party's 2023 sports-policy wording about Māori "genetic makeup being stronger", later removed from its website, against accusations of racism. - Ejected from the House several times (2021 haka during an argument with Judith Collins; 2023 haka welcoming Meka Whaitiri). - **2025–26 internal conflict:** as co-leader he was at the centre of the dispute in which president John Tamihere accused Kapa-Kingi and Ferris of plotting to replace the leaders; the national council expelled both in November 2025, which Ferris called "plainly unconstitutional". | | |

## Current status

**#5** on the Women's Rights Party list in 2026 (she was also #5 in 2023). Never an MP.

## Biography

Born 23 March 1943. A feminist economist with an MA from Oxford, where she campaigned for women's admission to the Oxford Union. She moved to New Zealand in 1969 and taught at Victoria University of Wellington, rising to associate professor of economics and gender & women's studies. She resigned when the university abolished gender and women's studies in a 2008–2010 restructuring. She wrote a 2000 report on the culture of the New Zealand Police and *Women and Economics* (2014), and played cricket for Middlesex and Wellington women's teams.

## Record & notable actions

- Has written widely on pay equity and living wages. She criticises the transgender rights movement and argues for classifying people by sex rather than gender.

## Controversies

None of significance found in the sources consulted.
